flaws: Water does not read as water. The vertical pale-blue cylinders drop straight from the upper tier's rim to the basin, so they look like columns holding up a gazebo roof. There is no arc, spray, splash or pooling to tell the eye it is falling water, and the piece reads as a pavilion or cake stand rather than a fountain.

Dark brand probe breaks the model. The central column and the inner faces of the upper tier render as a hard black 'T' shape against lime green, which reads as a glyph or rendering error rather than stone. The water stays lime on a lime basin with almost no contrast, so the pieces merge into one block.
Dark brand probe also maps the water to saturated lime, which reads as toxic slime. Brand colours are applied to semantic materials (water) without any constraint that keeps them plausible.

At max, three stacked tiers with near-identical proportions read as a wedding cake. The tiers get no change in jet style or height rhythm, so the top tier feels like a copy-paste rather than designed.
The size knob at maximum shows barely any visible change in footprint or height, so the knob does not earn its place.
The model sits small in the frame with a lot of empty canvas. At the default framing, details like the lamps and plaque are tiny.
The night mode lights only the lamp dots. The water, the obvious hero for a night glow, stays flat and dull.
grades.lesson: When an asset depicts a material the viewer must recognise (water, fire, glass, foliage), give it at least one shape cue that only that material has, such as arcs, splashes or translucency, and never let a brand colour override that material without a floor on contrast against adjacent parts. Then check every brand probe for accidental high-contrast shapes formed where brand colours meet.

flaws: Night mode turns all the water amber-orange. It reads as a fire or lava fountain rather than lit water. The glow overrides the water's own colour instead of brightening it.
The water jets are built from stacked, separated cylinders. At normal viewing size they read as bead chains or dotted lines, not continuous arcs of water.
At max knobs the middle-tier jet arcs crowd the top tier and cross it. Nothing visibly prevents jets from passing through the upper bowls.
Small yellow specks float on the basin rim and water surface (defaults and all presets). They read as stray artefacts, not designed lights.
The size knob at maximum barely changes the overall footprint or framing compared with defaults. Its range feels nearly inert.
The spire top option adds an unexplained orange cube cap that clashes with the stone and water palette.
The object fills under half the canvas at every setting, leaving a lot of dead space for a kit piece meant to sit on a grid tile.
In the light brand probe the saturated cyan water loses the 'pale blue' calm the brief asked for, and it overpowers the cream stone.
grades.lesson: When adding a night or emissive mode, derive each glowing part's colour from that part's own material hue (brighten or desaturate it) rather than applying one global light colour, so materials keep their identity in the dark.

flaws: Does not read as a fountain at any setting. The 'water' is a huge opaque stacked cone that dominates the mass, so the silhouette reads as a Buddhist stupa, temple or tiered cake rather than a plaza fountain.
No visible basin holding water. Nothing sits below a rim, and there are no jets, spill, or falling-water cues. The water sits on top of the stone like solid architecture.
The 'spire' top option makes the stupa reading definitive. It is a pointed stone finial, an architectural ornament rather than a fountain element.
Night mode makes the entire water mass glow amber/orange, so it reads as a lantern or lava rather than lit water. Water should stay cool-toned or show lit edges.
The brief asks for a central column with water as pale blue cylinders. The render inverts that ratio: water is the bulk and the column is barely present.
The unexplained orange/green/red/cyan block on the plinth looks like a random plaque or crate. Its purpose is unclear, and it swaps to arbitrary accent colours across presets.
At max knobs the third tier stacks into a taller wedding-cake or pagoda shape. The size change is barely perceptible, so the footprint does not visibly scale.
The asset occupies under half the canvas at every setting, which leaves lots of dead space for a hero kit piece.
The water colour knob, judging by the presets, lands on near-identical cyans and blues. There is little meaningful range.
grades.lesson: Before polishing, check the silhouette at thumbnail size against the object's single most recognisable cue (for a fountain: water contained below a basin rim). If the shape could be mistaken for a different well-known object, fix proportions before anything else.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bakery with a big bread-shaped sign, a bay window of loaves, a striped awning and a chimney. Knobs: wall, awning (primary role), sign colour, floors 1-3, chimney toggle, lights.

flaws: The bread sign, the hero element of the brief, collides with the first-floor left window box in every render: the oval clips through the planter and sill. It also sits half-hidden behind the awning, so it reads as a vague golden blob, not a loaf.

The storefront is crammed into the narrow front face. Sign, awning, bay window, loaves and door are stacked into one cluttered knot at the bottom right, while the large side wall has only two plain windows. Visual weight is badly unbalanced, and the bakery identity is illegible at thumbnail size.
The awning stripes are so short and fragmented that they read as a pile of boxes rather than a striped awning.

Dark brand probe: the walls go pure black. The left and right faces lose almost all shading separation and the building becomes a silhouette with a grey roof pasted on. The sign turns cyan, and a cyan bread sign makes no sense. The brand colours are being forced onto semantic and material surfaces that should stay neutral or bread-coloured.
Dark brand probe: a lime awning against black walls and a cyan sign looks like an error state, not an on-brand variant.
The Classic preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds nothing.
The sign colour knob is unconstrained even though the brief makes the sign bread-shaped. Any non-bread hue destroys the read, so the knob invites broken output.
At max floors the extra storeys simply repeat window boxes. The sign/planter collision persists, and the shopfront looks even smaller relative to the building.
The pavement slab only runs along the front edge and looks like a stray strip rather than a grounded base.
grades.lesson: Reserve an explicit clearance volume around the signature element (the thing the asset is named for) and check that no other parametric part (windows, planters, extra floors) can ever intrude into it; if the hero feature is clipped or occluded at defaults, nothing else matters.

flaws: The bread sign's rim renders as a jagged, sawtooth halo in every render (orange, pink, cyan). It looks like z-fighting or noisy offset geometry rather than a clean border, and it is the asset's hero feature.
The sign does not read as bread. It is a flat brown oval with a few pixel-block bumps, with no crust shape, scoring or loaf silhouette. The brief asks for a big bread-shaped sign.
The sign colour knob only tints the broken rim. The sign body stays the same brown, so the knob's effect is weak and it mostly amplifies the artifact.
The bay window of loaves is barely legible. It is crammed under the awning, which crowds into it, and the loaves are tiny brown slivers. The door is also mostly hidden behind the display box.
The awning sits low and intersects the shopfront massing. Its rear valance and the upper planter box visually collide.
Night mode is underwhelming. Only one upper window and the shop interior faintly glow. The sign is unlit and goes muddy, which is the opposite of what a bakery night state should do.
The floors=3 render shrinks the whole model, including the base plate, to fit the frame. For a 6 m grid kit piece this breaks visual scale parity with neighbouring pieces in thumbnails.
Tiny props on the left plinth edge, near the bench, are unreadable specks at this scale.
grades.lesson: Never build decorative outlines or rims as coplanar or jittered geometry. Give them real depth offset and a clean solid silhouette, then inspect the hero feature at thumbnail size in every colour variant before submitting.

flaws: At floors=3 the right face of the top storey has a lone red shutter sliver at the wall edge (around x≈313) with no window. Façade elements are clipped by the wall boundary instead of fitting inside it. This is a broken render.
At floors=3 the right upper wall becomes a tall, mostly blank cream slab with sparse, randomly placed windows. The building reads as stretched rather than designed for three storeys.
The 'big bread-shaped sign' from the brief reads as a small loaf lying flat on a tray on the extension roof. It does not stand up, face the street or read as signage at thumbnail size.
The 'bay window of loaves' from the brief is not legible. The shopfront under the awning is a dark recess with a few tiny brown specks, so the key bakery identifier is missing.
In Blueberry the lit right-hand upper wall is nearly the same value as the background. The silhouette dissolves and the wall almost looks absent, with only a hairline edge.
The side awning on the right face is plain white while the front awning is striped. The two look like different parts and the inconsistency reads as a mistake.
The sign colour knob tints only the thin tray under the loaf, and the loaf stays brown. In the dark brand probe this produces a cyan sliver that adds noise without making the sign read as branded.
The front awning hangs low over the door and hides most of the entrance, so the shopfront entry is hard to read at defaults.
grades.lesson: When a knob changes a building's size or floor count, compute window, shutter and trim positions from the actual face dimensions for that knob value. Skip any element that would not fit entirely on its face rather than letting the face edge clip it. Then render every floor-count extreme and check each façade for partial fragments.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A corner cafe with a glass front, two outdoor tables with parasols and chairs on the pavement side (z 0 to 1.5). Knobs: wall, parasol colour, tables 0-3, floors 1-2, lights.

flaws: At max, tables=3 does not fit the pavement strip. The third parasol cuts into the green storefront pilaster and awning, and the parasols overlap each other. Chairs crowd together and push toward the glass, so the furniture breaks out of the z 0 to 1.5 pavement zone in the brief.
The Bistro preset renders identically to the defaults. A preset that changes nothing is dead weight.
The max render looks like the defaults apart from table count. Floors is either already at 2 by default or does nothing visible, so the floors knob's range is not demonstrated.
The 'glass front' reads as opaque flat yellow panels in daylight, with no transparency, reflection or visible interior. The ground-floor side windows look like painted boards rather than glazing.
The shopfront is cluttered at defaults. The striped awnings, parasols, window boxes and a small facade sign all pile onto the same corner, and the left parasol visually collides with the glazing.

In the dark brand probe, the white trim and pilaster merge into the white pavement slab, so the shopfront frame disappears. The lime-and-white awning stripes are nearly invisible, and lime parasols over pale yellow glass have almost no contrast. The front loses its structure.
The night mode turns the walls a muddy taupe-grey that reads as a different, dirtier material rather than the same wall colour under night light.
At the left gable end there is no visible gable wall and the roof face sits ambiguously, so the roof form reads unclear.
grades.lesson: When a count knob places repeated props, derive their positions from the actual free footprint at the maximum count. Assert they clear the building and each other, or cap the knob at what physically fits. Never let the top of a range push objects into walls.

flaws: Gable roof at defaults: the flat white canopy over the shopfront has the same pure-white fill as the roof slope it abuts, with no edge or tone break. The two merge into one ambiguous white mass that looks like the canopy is cutting into the roof.
The 'glass front' does not read as glass. It shows as an opaque brown interior behind grey bars, with no transparency, reflection or tint cue.
Pale grey horizontal members float across the storefront. They overshoot the left column, forming a disconnected bracket that looks like a modelling leftover.
Not a corner cafe as briefed. Only one face has the glazed front; the corner and side elevation are plain wall with a single small window.
Max range (2 floors): the upper-floor front window sits on top of the canopy plane, and the pink sign plank overlaps the canopy edge. Upper geometry is not re-anchored when floors increase.
Max range: upper windows are inconsistent, with one lit yellow and one unlit grey-blue on the same elevation.
Max range: stray thin posts stand at the pavement edge, and the third table set crowds the others.
Night mode: walls and roof collapse into one muddy taupe with little separation. The glass shopfront does not glow, only the door and a lamp do, so the cafe reads as closed.
Dark brand probe: walls and roof both go near-black, and the building becomes a heavy silhouette. The gable window and wall detail are almost lost, and front and side faces barely separate.
The roof's lit planes are blank white with a thin grey edge. Massing relies on outline rather than shading, which looks unfinished next to a 'palette-matched' kit.
grades.lesson: Anchor every attached element (canopies, signs, upper windows) to the live geometry of its host for every floor-count and roof combination, and give adjacent surfaces distinct tones or edges, so parts never interpenetrate or visually merge into one flat mass.

flaws: At every range knob at maximum (3 tables, 2 floors), the third parasol is half-buried in the shopfront and only a sliver pokes out past the corner. The table sets also crowd into each other, with chairs overlapping at the front edge of the pavement. The count knob places instances without checking clearance against the building.
The glass front and fascia carry scattered white pixel specks, presumably meant as decals or pendant lights. At render size they read as noise or artifacts rather than intentional detail.

Outdoor furniture reads as loosely grouped. The table tops are mostly hidden under the parasols, and at defaults one chair pair on the right does not clearly belong to either parasol, so 'two tables with parasols' is not legible.

Dark brand probe maps the wall to near-black. The gable end becomes a flat void that swallows the vent and pilaster detail, and the black chimney fights the unchanged terracotta roof. Brand dark is being applied to the largest surface instead of an accent.
Flat roof option leaves the chimney as a saturated red box that reads as neither chimney nor rooftop plant. It is the most attention-grabbing element on an otherwise neutral roof.
Trim colour changes with presets and probes but is not among the briefed knobs. It is unclear whether it is exposed or derived, and the derived dark-probe result (light grey trim) looks unplanned.
grades.lesson: When a count knob adds instances, recompute their layout from the free footprint at every count and test the maximum against the building's real geometry. Nothing may intersect walls or other instances, and nothing may spill past the plot edge.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A narrow ramen shop with noren curtain strips over the door, a vertical sign and paper lanterns that glow. Knobs: wall, curtain colour, lantern count 0-4, roof gable/flat, lights.

flaws: The noren curtain, a core feature in the brief, is barely visible at the fixed isometric camera. It is buried behind the vertical sign and lanterns, so the curtain-colour knob has almost no visible effect.
The storefront is cramped and overlapping. The vertical sign sits in front of the awning and partly hides the lanterns and doorway. At lantern count 4 (max render), the lanterns crowd into the sign.
The sign glyphs read as garbled pseudo-kana rather than legible ラーメン. A buyer would notice.

The side-facade windows are flat orange squares with no frames or mullions, unlike the detailed front windows. At max storeys, one side window randomly turns grey-blue while the others stay lit, which looks like a bug rather than a choice.
The flat-roof variant leaves the chimney vent half-sunk and clipped into the roof edge at the back corner.

The dark brand probe maps the dark colour to the walls, giving pure black walls under a near-white roof. The roof loses its edge against the pale background, the lime lanterns clash, and the piece no longer reads as a warm ramen shop.
In the light brand probe, the hip face of the roof shades to near-black, which is harsh and unlike the rest of the kit.
The Shoyu preset renders identically to the defaults, so it is a wasted preset.
In night mode the lanterns do not visibly glow; only the windows do, despite the brief calling for glowing lanterns.
grades.lesson: Verify that every feature named in the brief is unoccluded and readable from the kit's fixed camera at default and maximum counts; if a signature element is hidden behind other geometry, move or scale it, because its knob is otherwise meaningless.

flaws: The paper lanterns do not glow in the night render. They read as dull dark-blue discs while the windows and sign light up, so a headline feature of the brief is missing.
The awning's right end runs into the vertical sign. In every render the awning and lanterns cover the lower glyphs, so only about one and a half characters of the sign are readable.
At max storeys/lanterns the lanterns crowd into the sign column and the sign glyphs are cut off. The ground-floor detailing collides instead of reflowing.

With the flat roof, the old chimney/vent cap is left half-sunk into the back parapet corner, and there is a stray dark notch on the left parapet edge. This is a visible leftover from the gable variant.
The dark brand probe maps the accent to a lime curtain and cyan sign on charcoal walls. It looks garish and off-palette next to the warm town kit, and the curtain emblem turns into a black blob.
The brief asks for 'narrow' and noren 'strips', but the massing is the same squat footprint as a generic town house. The curtain reads as two flat panels rather than distinct strips.
Lanterns are tiny and tucked behind the curtain at defaults, so the lantern count knob barely changes the silhouette.
grades.lesson: Position attached details (signs, awnings, lanterns, vents, chimneys) from the actual bounds of their neighbours under the current knob values, and remove or move them when a variant changes their host. Then check every preset, extreme and choice render for overlaps and leftovers before submitting.

flaws: Roof 'flat': the gable roof's chimney vent is still drawn after the swap. Its cap sits squashed into the back corner of the parapet, a leftover from the gable geometry that reads as a rendering glitch.

Dark brand probe: wall and roof both go to near-identical mid-greys, so the building looks like an unpainted grey model. The cyan sign and green noren sit on it as unrelated accents rather than a coherent palette, and the warm Oasis Town look is lost.

The vertical sign hangs over the door bay and its lower end runs into the awning. It partly hides the noren, which is the feature the brief centres on. At the maximum render the sign also crosses the floor-band line.

The shopfront is squeezed onto the narrow right face while the wide left face is blank wall with generic windows. At kit scale the ramen identity (noren, lanterns, sign) is tiny and hard to read compared with the large plain massing.
Sign glyphs are pseudo-katakana squiggles. They read as fake text to anyone who knows Japanese, which is a risk for a culturally specific asset.
Night mode: the lanterns wash out to pale cream instead of glowing warm orange, with no halo or light spill. The 'paper lanterns that glow' from the brief are weaker than the windows.
At 4 lanterns the cluster runs to the very end of the awning and crowds against the building edge rather than being spaced along it.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob swaps a major component (e.g. roof type), re-derive every attached detail from the new component or drop it. Never leave accessories positioned for the old geometry.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bookshop with a green front, shelves of coloured book spines in the window and a hanging sign. Knobs: front colour, book colours seed, floors 1-3, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: sign

flaws: At defaults the ground floor between the left wall and the green shopfront reads as a missing wall. A pale wedge of floor/slab shows up to the first-floor ledge, so the building looks like an unintended cutaway rather than a closed volume.

The dark brand probe makes that void glaring. Black walls frame a bright white wedge, and the brand colour floods the entire wall mass, producing a harsh black-and-lime house rather than a branded shopfront.

At max floors the whole model is rescaled to fit the frame. The footprint, shopfront and base shrink, so the piece no longer sits on the 6 m kit grid at the same scale as town-shop.mjs, which defeats its purpose as a block-kit piece.
Preset 'Bottle' renders pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no value.
The hanging sign the brief asks for is a tiny yellow square that is barely readable as a sign at any setting.
The upper-floor front on the right face has a lot of dead cream wall, and the window placement looks sparse and unbalanced next to the busy shopfront.
grades.lesson: Before shipping a 3D/isometric building, flat-shade it and check from the camera angle that every face a viewer expects to be solid is actually closed. Exposed slabs or floor plates where a wall should be read as broken geometry, and brand recolours will only make the hole more obvious.

flaws: The brief's defining feature is weak. The book-spine window is a narrow slot to the right of the door, and the books read as coloured noise at render size. Most of the shopfront facade is blank green, partly hidden by the table, so the piece reads as 'green shop' more than 'bookshop'.
The hanging sign is a tiny, illegible blob in every render. It adds no identity.
Dark brand probe: the cream upper facade and side wall turn muddy grey-taupe, which sits too close to the grey roof. The whole house looks drab and low-contrast.
Dark brand probe: the lime door, frame and shutters merge into the lime front. The door and window joinery lose definition.

Light brand probe and the Oxblood preset also shift the neutral side wall (to greige and cool grey). The 'neutral' surfaces are not stable across colour settings, which works against matching a shared town palette.
At max floors the upper storeys are fine. However, the shopfront fascia and display stay small relative to a now-tall building, so the ground floor gets weaker as floors increase.
grades.lesson: Whatever the brief names as the asset's identity (here, a window full of books) must take up a dominant, legible share of the main facade at thumbnail size. Supporting surfaces should keep stable neutral colours so brand-colour changes cannot muddy them.

flaws: Dark brand probe is garish. The shopfront turns neon lime with cyan fascia panels, and the shutters go lime too. It clashes hard with the muted beige, cream and slate palette and reads as broken theming, not a dark brand. A designer would be embarrassed to ship this.
The shop has no visible entrance. The ground floor is two display bays split by a pillar, with no door in any render. That is a basic credibility gap for a town-kit shop piece.

The 'every knob at max' render frames the building smaller in the canvas and fills the windows with pale, noisy spines. Book-colour range at max loses the warm curated look of the defaults and the shelves read as clutter.
The Ink and Oxblood presets only swap the front colour. That is acceptable but thin.
The night mode is under-lit for a shop: only one side window glows. The shop windows, fascia and hanging sign stay dull, so the bookshop barely reads at night.
The hanging sign and fascia carry no glyph or identity mark, so 'bookshop' relies entirely on the window contents.
grades.lesson: When mapping a brand colour onto an asset, keep the role and luminance the slot was designed for. Clamp the incoming colour's lightness and saturation into the band the rest of the palette lives in, and derive trims from it. A raw or auto-lightened brand hue should never be dropped into a large surface, because a dark brand that comes out neon breaks the whole piece.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A park bench with a slatted seat and back, optional planter boxes at each end. Footprint 2x1. Knobs: wood colour, frame colour, planters toggle, length 1.5-3 m.

warnings: colour knobs without a brand role: wood, frame, bloom

flaws: Max-length render is broken: the added middle support shows as a grey block sticking up through the centre of the seat slats, and a stub pokes above the back rail.
Light brand probe tints the wood slats, the armrests and the planter boxes all the same teal. The bench and planters merge into one plastic-looking mass with no material hierarchy.

Dark brand probe shows white frame posts on a near-white background, so the legs almost disappear. Lime is applied to both the wood and the planters, which looks garish. The flowers become cyan, which does not read as a plant.
Brand colour overrides the 'wood colour' role entirely, so the bench stops reading as a wooden bench, the core identity of the asset.
Night variant crushes the planter front faces to near-black against the navy background, losing their form. Nothing on the asset actually glows, so the 'lit parts' mode adds nothing.
The Park preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, a wasted preset.
Planter colour has no knob of its own and is tied to other roles. The planters-off state is never shown, so the toggle cannot be verified.
The right armrest visually sits on top of the planter rim at default length, which reads as interpenetration rather than clearance.
Only three back slats with wide gaps make the back read sparse next to the dense seat.
grades.lesson: Any part generated or repositioned by a size knob (mid supports, repeated legs, spacers) must derive its position and height from the same dimensions as the surfaces it attaches to. Render every size knob at its extremes and check for parts poking through other geometry before submitting.

flaws: Scale is not fixed. At maximum length the whole model shrinks to fit the frame. The planters, lamp caps and leg sections are visibly smaller than at defaults. For a kit piece that must match town-shop.mjs on a 6 m grid, this breaks scale consistency with the other kit assets.
The length knob gives no visible proof that the bench honours the 2x1 footprint. Because of the auto-fit, a 3 m bench and a 1.5 m bench cannot be compared in grid units.
The lamp-topped back posts were not in the brief. They make the bench read partly as a lamp fixture. They appear only on the rear posts, which looks arbitrary next to the plain front posts.
In the dark brand probe, the brand colour is applied raw to the planter bodies. The result is an eye-searing flat lime box that dominates the piece. No tint or shade tempering is applied.
In Night, the wood and frame collapse into near-identical dark mauve-grey tones. The slats and the bench silhouette lose definition against the background, so only the lamps read clearly.
The planters sit tight against the armrests. From this angle it is ambiguous whether they touch or interpenetrate, and no clear gap separates them.
The planters toggle is not demonstrated in any render, so the off state cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: Kit pieces meant to sit on a shared grid must render at a fixed world-to-pixel scale. Never auto-fit the camera to model bounds, or size knobs will silently rescale everything else and break consistency with sibling assets.

flaws: The seat is structurally wrong at defaults. Only the front seat slats are present, and a gap between them and the backrest shows the white pavement through the seat, so it reads as a broken bench.
Seat and backrest lengths don't match. The seat slats run past the right end of the backrest and frame, and a stray slat end juts out at the left like a mismatched armrest.
At maximum length the far end of the bench runs into the far planter, so seat and back geometry intersects the planter box.
At maximum length the near planter sits right on the slab edge and appears to hang over it. Planter placement is not tied to the bench length.
The far planter is mostly hidden behind the backrest at defaults and the presets, so the 'planters at each end' feature barely reads from the kit camera.
The bench looks oversized for a 2x1 footprint on a 6 m grid. A 1.5–3 m bench should occupy a much smaller share of a 12 m slab, which suggests the scale doesn't match the town-shop kit.
No render shows planters toggled off, so that knob can't be verified.
grades.lesson: When a parametric dimension changes, derive every attached part (slats, supports, end accessories) from the same computed extents, and check at both minimum and maximum that parts neither overlap nor leave unintended gaps.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bus stop shelter with a roof, glass back panel, bench, timetable sign and a pole sign. Footprint 3x2. Knobs: frame colour, roof colour, sign colour, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to defaults. The range knobs are either inert or missing, so nothing in the geometry (depth, bench length, roof overhang, pole height) is adjustable.
The Tram preset is identical to defaults, which makes it a wasted preset that adds no variety.
The brief asks for a timetable sign in addition to the pole sign. No legible timetable panel appears on the shelter, only the plain glass side panel and the pole sign.

The night mode barely reads. The pole lamp glows faintly, the sign is not lit, and the curved roof has no underside light. The peaked roof does have a light strip, so lighting is inconsistent between roof shapes.
In the dark brand probe the frame maps to near-white. The posts and bench legs nearly disappear against the white platform and light background, and the structure loses definition.
The peaked roof variant swaps the pole sign to a different graphic and lowers it with no knob controlling this. A choice knob is causing unrelated, unpredictable side effects.
The stair-stepped voxel curve on the barrel roof looks noisy at this size compared with the clean planes elsewhere.
grades.lesson: Before submitting, diff every preset and the extreme-knob render against defaults. Any render that is identical means a knob or preset does nothing, so either wire it to visible geometry or remove it. Also check that every component named in the brief is actually present and recognisable.

flaws: The 'light' is a strip lying on the outside of the roof slope. At defaults it reads as a stray plank. In the night render the glow sits on top of the roof instead of lighting the waiting area under the canopy, which is physically illogical.
The glass back panel renders as an opaque slate-blue slab. Nothing reads as glass: no transparency, reflection highlight or mullions.
The bench, a brief requirement, is almost entirely hidden behind the side panel. Only a sliver of brown slats is visible at the fixed camera angle.
The Harbour preset's white roof nearly disappears against the pale background, so the shelter loses its top silhouette.
'Every range knob at max' looks almost identical to defaults apart from a slight roof and scale change. The range knobs don't produce meaningful variation.
The gable roof is heavy and house-like for a bus shelter. The twin-roof option reads as two disconnected roof pieces with an awkward valley.
The pole sign and timetable details are tiny and turn into dark smudges at this scale.
The shelter occupies only the left half of the 3x2 platform, leaving a large empty slab that looks unfinished rather than composed.
grades.lesson: Place every functional detail where it would physically sit and face the viewer (lights under canopies, benches in view, glass visibly transparent), then check from the fixed camera that each item named in the brief is actually readable at defaults.

flaws: roofShape 'pitched' silently removes the roof-mounted sign box, so the sign colour knob then only affects the small pole sign; the variant reads as a different, less-branded shelter rather than the same shelter with a different roof
Bench is mostly lost behind the glass and frame at every view; at night it nearly disappears, weakening one of the brief's listed components
Front bin sits tight against the front corner post; at max ranges it crowds and nearly overlaps the post, reading as a near-collision
Daytime floor marking (lit patch outline) is so faint it reads as a rendering artefact rather than an intentional bay marking
Roof is a flat untextured slab with no fascia or gutter detail; acceptable for the kit's flat style but the plainest surface in the piece
grades.lesson: When a choice knob removes an element, make sure every other knob that styled that element still has a visible target in that variant; otherwise relocate the element rather than deleting it.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A boxy toy hatchback car with windows, wheels as dark cylinders lying sideways (use boxes for wheels), headlights. Footprint 4x2. Knobs: body colour (primary), roof rack toggle, lights.

flaws: A large dark-grey slab juts out of the rear flank in every render. It cuts across the rear side window and the body side like a misplaced fender or an open door. It reads as broken geometry, not a design feature.
At max, the slab grows and covers even more of the side window and door, so the defect gets worse at the extremes.

The roof rack is a set of flat white planks that cover almost the whole roof and overhang the windscreen. It reads as a second roof, not a rack. In the dark-brand probe it becomes a heavy lavender lid that dominates the car.
The red tail-light block sticks up above the rear body line instead of sitting flush in the bodywork. It looks bolted on as an afterthought.
The silhouette reads as a tall SUV or station wagon, not the boxy hatchback the brief asks for.
Preset 'Sky' renders identically to the defaults, so it adds nothing.
'Tram' is a confusing name for a car colourway.
At Night the white roof panels go flat grey and lose definition against the body, making the top read as one muddy slab.
Small slivers of the secondary colour poke out at the front wing and the A-pillar base, leaving visible seams at the body edges.
grades.lesson: Before shipping, inspect the model from its main viewing angle at defaults and at every extreme. Check that each part sits within or flush with the body silhouette and does not intersect glazing or other parts unintentionally. A single protruding or interpenetrating box reads as a bug, and it will appear in every variant.

flaws: Core geometry is wrong at defaults. A single large flat body slab runs over where the cabin should be. The windshield and side windows poke up through it like loose panels, and the roof (white panel) sits behind and visually below that slab. The car never reads as a hatchback with a greenhouse; it reads as a box with glass shards stuck in it.

There is no readable cabin silhouette, no A/C-pillar stepping and no hatch slope. The 'hatchback' brief is not met. Only the pickup variant has a cabin sitting correctly on top of the body, which proves the default stacking is a bug rather than a style.
The front clutter (black grille block, bumper, black fender boxes) is a pile of disconnected dark blocks. It does not read as a nose. The headlights are tiny chips half-hidden behind the bumper.
At the all-max extreme the body stretches, but the front wheel and fender block crowd into the bumper. The same buried-window problem persists.

The roof panel's colour role is inconsistent across renders: white at defaults, salmon in the light probe, lavender in the dark probe, flat grey at night. It reads as a random accent rather than glass, a sunroof or a roof rack. The roof rack toggle it presumably represents is not legible as a rack in any render.
The wheels are flat square plates with white hubs flush on black boxes. They read more as speakers than as tyres, even within a blocky kit.
In the dark brand probe, the acid-lime body with lavender roof is garish, and the lime-on-light-grey edges lose definition. The asset does not hold its tonal shading well on very light hues.
grades.lesson: Before polishing, check the default silhouette for correct vertical stacking. Every part that should sit on top of another (cabin on body, roof on cabin, glass inside its frame) must have its base at or above the supporting part's top, never buried inside it. Verify this by eye at the default camera angle before rendering variants.

flaws: The hatchback silhouette is broken at defaults. A single flat slab at roof height covers almost the whole car. The windshield and side window poke up through it as floating grey panels, and the white roof panel sits behind and below it. The cabin reads as swallowed by the body rather than sitting on it.
The model does not read as a hatchback. It looks like a flat-topped van or wagon block with no stepped cabin volume, which fails the brief.

The front fascia is confusing. A black U-shaped bracket sits on the hood front and partly hides the headlights. The front-left wheel box protrudes past the bumper line, so the nose reads as a cluster of unrelated parts.

The white roof panel (presumably the roof rack) is the brightest element in the scene. It pulls focus and does not look like a rack. In the brand probes it turns into a flat salmon or purple slab with no rack structure.
The 'max' render only stretches length. Wheels drift inward and the same intersecting slab or window problem gets worse. Nothing about the extreme looks more intentional.
The pickup variant reads much better than the default car. This shows the cabin and body stacking in the main style is wrong, not a stylistic choice.
In the dark brand probe (lime body), the headlights and side trim lose contrast against the body colour. In the night render the cabin top turns muddy grey and the bracket blends into the body.
grades.lesson: Before shipping a stacked block model, check the vertical order of every volume from the actual camera angle. Lower body, then cabin, then roof and accessories. No panel should be taller than the volume it is meant to sit on or in. Intersecting slabs that hide the cabin destroy the silhouette that makes the object recognisable.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A pair of vending machines with lit fronts and rows of coloured drinks. Footprint 2x1. Knobs: machine colours, machines 1-3, lights.

errors: knobs with no visible effect: bodyC

flaws: The rear (blue) machine does not reach the slab in any render. Its body stops roughly a third of the way up, with bare floor visible beneath it. Its dispensing tray floats in mid-air in front of nothing. This reads as broken geometry, not a stylistic choice.
At max machine count the same bug repeats on the green third machine. White floor shows through the gap between the blue and green bodies, so the back machines read as hollow, legless shells.
The rear machines' side faces are thin slivers, so they read as flat billboards rather than solid boxes next to the fully modelled front machine.

The canopy is supported by a single back-left post, and its right end is cantilevered with no visible support. This is structurally implausible for a kit piece meant to sit beside town-shop scale buildings.

Scale looks off for the 6 m grid. Each machine is several metres wide and fills most of the 2x1 footprint, where real vending machines are about 1 m wide by 1.8 m tall. It is unlikely to match town-shop.mjs proportions.
The 'Classic' preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it wastes a preset slot.
Drink colours stay fixed in both brand probes. In the dark brand probe the lime machine against the fixed purple/pink/green drinks looks uncoordinated rather than branded.
The 'open' shelter option changes the machine tops (adding overhanging roofs) as well as removing the canopy. The knob does more than its label says.
grades.lesson: When a parametric piece repeats an object N times, generate every instance from the same ground-anchored geometry and check the render that each one actually touches the floor plane and is a closed solid from the camera angle. Back-row copies are where clipping and floating parts hide.

flaws: Depth-sorting error in every sheltered render (defaults, all presets, max, night, both brand probes). The left machine's top face is drawn over the roof, so it reads as a box punching through the canopy.
The roof is not a continuous slab. A visible notch sits where the red machine top overlaps it, and the front fascia beam then crosses over that top. This creates contradictory occlusion.
The shelter's front-left post and beam cut across the face of the first machine. This crowds its side panel and makes the left edge of the composition read as tangled rather than framed.
At 3 machines (max), the left frame shows a doubled post-and-beam junction. The shelter does not cleanly re-fit the wider row. The red machine's top again sits over the frame beam.
The drinks are tiny and limited to a narrow strip. At kit scale the 'rows of coloured drinks' read as noise rather than a clear product display.
Night mode only warms the front panels. The roof and frame stay flat with no light spill, so the 'lit fronts' feature is underwhelming for its prominence in the brief.
The colour knobs accept hues like full-saturation lime with no harmonisation. The light-brand teal roof also overpowers the machines. There is no guard to keep the piece within the town-shop palette.
grades.lesson: When composing stacked isometric parts (machines under a roof), sort and occlusion-test by the actual 3D overlap rather than by draw order of components. Then render a check at each count/size extreme to confirm nothing beneath a covering surface ever paints over it.

flaws: Light-spill pads are off by one. At defaults only the red machine gets a cream pad and the blue one gets none. At 3 machines, red and blue get pads but green does not. In the night render a single machine casts a glowing pool while its neighbour casts nothing, which reads as a bug.
The pad renders as a cream mat in daylight, where no light is visible, so it looks like a stray decal rather than a light effect.

Raising the machine count squeezes the units into the fixed 2x1 footprint, so each machine gets narrower. Per-unit scale drifts between settings, which works against the brief's 'matching town-shop scale'.
Night mode washes each door to a flat cream panel and darkens the drinks into muddy tones. The 'rows of coloured drinks' read worst in exactly the mode meant to show them off.
On the side panel only the top strip glows at night, and the large panel below goes dark and dead. This gives an unbalanced lighting hierarchy.
Drinks are generic tiny blocks with little variation, so the fronts feel repetitive at close inspection.
grades.lesson: When an asset repeats a per-unit sub-part (lights, pads, shadows, labels) across a count knob, generate it inside the same per-unit loop as the unit itself, and check every count value so no unit ends up missing its part.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A red telephone booth with glass panes and a lit crown sign. Footprint 1x1. Knobs: colour, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: sign

flaws: The roof geometry is muddled. It reads as two intersecting gables with an odd notch and a stray second peak behind the finial, not a clean hip or the iconic domed booth top. The silhouette, which carries the object's identity, looks like a modelling error.

The brief's 'lit crown sign' is not delivered. The crowns are tiny amber tabs stuck on the roof slopes that read as stray stickers. In the Night render they go dull brown instead of glowing; only the header panels light up.
The two header signs are inconsistent: cream on the left face, near-white on the right. Their 'lettering' is a row of black ticks that never reads as TELEPHONE, even at the 512 px hero size.
The right-face glazing has a few random pure-white panes mixed in with tinted ones. It reads as noise rather than deliberate reflection.
In the dark brand probe, lime body with pale mullions and a cream sign leaves almost no value contrast. The window grid and signage wash out, and the piece looks garish rather than branded.
At range maximums the booth narrows and the roof gets squashed, with the sign glyphs shrinking. Proportions drift away from the town-shop scale the brief asks to match.
Preset 'Classic' renders identically to the defaults, so it is a wasted preset slot. Flat-roof mode adds a saturated yellow-orange parapet that clashes with the kit palette.
grades.lesson: Before shipping, check the two things that define a small kit object at thumbnail size: its signature silhouette and every feature the brief names. Confirm the silhouette is geometrically clean from the fixed camera, and confirm each named feature is clearly legible and behaves as described (e.g. 'lit' parts actually glow) in every mode, including night and both brand probes.

flaws: The crown sign is broken in every render. The word is split across the corner, with its halves in the wrong reading order: the left face shows 'JNE' and the right face shows 'PHO', so it reads as garbled nonsense instead of 'PHONE'. The 'O' is also clipped into a 'J'.
The 'TAXI' label choice has the same fault. It reads 'XI' then 'TA' left to right, and the 'A' glyph renders with stray pixels like an 'Ä'.
The 'Every range knob at its maximum' render is practically indistinguishable from defaults. The range knobs either do nothing visible or have ranges too timid to matter.
The 'label' choice offers TAXI on a phone booth. It is a semantically odd option, and the core label is broken anyway.
Sign glyphs are tiny chunky pixel text. Even if spelled correctly they would barely read at kit scale.
The dark brand probe came out as a bright lime that is not meaningfully darker than the light probe, so it gives little evidence of how the asset behaves under a genuinely dark brand colour.
The booth occupies a small portion of the frame with a large empty margin. That is acceptable for a grid kit piece, but it weakens the presentation.
Positives that do not offset the defect: the night glow, colour presets, flat-roof variant, plinth and crown details are tidy.
grades.lesson: When text wraps around a 3D object's corner or sits on multiple faces, render the full word on each visible face (or verify reading order from the camera's viewpoint). Never split a word across faces, because isometric projection reverses or garbles the order and the asset ships with unreadable signage.

flaws: The 'TELEPHONE' sign panel is filled with jagged, misaligned dark bar clusters that read as scribbles or rendering glitches, not as lettering or as a deliberate abstraction. It is the focal detail at eye level and looks broken at defaults and in every variant.

The crown ornaments are shapeless yellow-orange lumps with no recognisable crown silhouette. The brief calls out a lit crown sign as a feature, but it reads as noise, and in the night render it goes dull brown instead of glowing.

The dark brand probe renders as a saturated lime green with a cold grey sign panel. It does not read as a dark brand colour, so either the brand colour is being lightened or the mapping is off. Either way, a designer cannot trust the colour knob to carry their brand faithfully.
The roof-top finial is a tiny undefined nub that turns into a muddy dot at night.
Apart from the sign, the body, glazing, door handle, plinth, flat-roof variant and pane-density extreme are clean and consistent. The asset is let down by its signature details, not its structure.
grades.lesson: Never fake text with randomised or jittered bar shapes. At small render sizes, either draw legible lettering on a clean baseline or use evenly spaced, aligned stripes that read as an intentional abstraction. Scrambled glyph blocks always look like a rendering bug.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A traffic light pole with three lamps on an arm over the road. Footprint 1x1. Knobs: pole colour, active light choice red/amber/green, arm length.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: button, lights

flaws: Night render is broken. The active red lamp and the pedestrian signal glow cream/white instead of red, so the defining read of a traffic light is lost at night.
Night mode also washes the unlit amber and green lamps into near-identical dark smudges, so you cannot tell which aspect is active.
At defaults the 'lit' red lamp reads as a pale salmon/pink block with a white rectangular glyph stamped on it. It looks like a texture artifact, not a lit lens.
The lit green lamp at 'active=green' is a pale mint that reads weakly against the dark housing.
Dark brand probe turns the pole and arm near-white on a near-white ground. The main structural silhouette almost vanishes and the pole edges lose definition.
Brand colour is applied to the signal backplate and push button. These are functional/regulatory colours, so the brand probe yields a cyan backplate that no longer reads as street hardware.
Max-range render shrinks the whole piece in frame rather than holding grid scale. It is hard to judge whether the 1x1 footprint and 6 m grid alignment survive a long arm.
Framing at defaults leaves the asset small and pushed up-left with large dead space, which weakens it as a showcase thumbnail.
grades.lesson: When a material switches to an emissive/glow state, preserve its semantic hue (red stays red, green stays green) and only raise brightness/bloom; never let a lighting mode collapse coloured signals to a shared warm white.

flaws: Night mode breaks the asset's core meaning. The active red lamp glows a washed-out cream/white instead of red, so you can no longer tell which signal is lit. The pedestrian head glows the same generic warm white, and the push-button box glows too.
The 'Classic' preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it is a wasted preset slot.
Arm length at maximum is only modestly longer than the default, so the range is too timid to cover wider roads.
At max arm length the framing scales the whole model down: the pole and lamps look smaller and thinner. That undermines the fixed 6 m grid scale a kit piece must hold.
Backplate trim behaves inconsistently across the brand probes. It stays default yellow under the light brand but switches to cyan under the dark brand.
The unlit amber lamp reads as muddy brown at defaults. The lamp lenses are small relative to the housing, so the signal state is weak at kit viewing distance.
The amber active state is not demonstrated, so its rendering is unverified.
grades.lesson: When a lighting mode such as night or emissive glow is applied, derive each glow from that element's own semantic hue rather than a shared warm-white emissive. Then check that colour-coded states stay distinguishable in every lighting mode.

flaws: The default active state is unreadable. The red and green lamps both look fully lit, and only amber reads as off. On a traffic light, the active-lamp state is the whole point, and at defaults you cannot tell which lamp is on.
Off lamps are not dimmed enough. In the 'green' choice the red lamp still reads as saturated red, so the on/off contrast is weak.
The night render breaks the signal's meaning. The lit lamps glow cream or white instead of their own hue, so a red signal reads as a white or yellow light. The pedestrian head shows the same problem.
The pole almost disappears against the night background. The base plinth and backplate border carry the whole silhouette.
The Civic and Tramline presets change only the pole colour. They add almost nothing beyond the colour knob, so the preset range is thin.

With the maximum arm length the head extends well past what reads as a 1x1 footprint, and the crosswalk is baked into the piece. That is questionable for a grid kit, where crossings belong to road tiles.
The crosswalk stripes have a faint beige outline that looks like an edge artefact rather than an intentional detail.
grades.lesson: Treat any on/off or active state as the asset's core signal. Make 'off' clearly dark and desaturated, and make emissive glow keep the hue of the part it lights. Then check that the active state reads correctly in every lighting mode, including night, before you submit.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A striped lighthouse on a rocky base with a glowing lamp room. Footprint 4x4. Knobs: stripe colours, height 8-14 m, stripes 2-5, lights.

flaws: The model fills only about a third of the 512 canvas at defaults and less at max height, so the detail (window sills, door lamp, rock caps) is tiny and the frame is mostly empty.
At max height the whole piece renders smaller to fit, so the base and lamp room shrink on screen and look less consistent beside other kit pieces at the same zoom.
Dark brand probe: brand white goes onto the lantern roof, gallery and hut roof. Against the pale background the top silhouette weakens, and the lamp glow loses contrast against the white cap.
Dark brand probe: the hut walls turn black, so the brown door reads poorly. The hut's role colour changes identity between probes (cream in the defaults, black here).
Window sills are flat dark grey bars that read as floating ledges more than sills.
The green caps on the rocks are ambiguous. They read as buttons or lily pads rather than grass or moss.
grades.lesson: Map brand colours to roles, not to every surface: reserve the brand's lightest and darkest values for accent parts, and keep focal and emissive elements (lamps, glass, doors) on fixed contrast-safe neutrals so they stay legible whatever the brand pair is.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A food truck with a serving hatch, awning flap, menu board and a little roof sign. Footprint 5x2.5. Knobs: body colour, awning colour, sign colour, hatch open toggle, lights.

flaws: The roof sign's pixel lettering is illegible in every render. It reads as scrambled 'E:AT'-like glyphs with stray red and yellow blocks breaking up the strokes, so the truck's most prominent identifying feature looks broken.

The serving hatch is dominated by a heavy dark-grey slab running diagonally across the body below the awning. It reads as a chassis bar slicing through the hatch, not as a counter or flap, and buries the interior detail.
The interior behind the hatch (white counter blocks, small yellow and green bits, vertical posts) is a cluttered jumble at the default scale. No readable food-service props emerge.
The front wheel sits isolated at the front corner beneath the cab, far from the rear axle, with no visible chassis linking them. The vehicle looks like it is floating on detached blocks.
The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to the defaults. Either the asset has no continuous knobs or they do nothing, so there is no scale or proportion control.
The hatch open toggle from the brief is never shown closed. Nothing demonstrates that the toggle works.
In the Tram preset the awning washes out to pale pink and white with almost no stripe contrast, so it disappears against the white interior.
In the dark brand probe the black body swallows the cab, door and side detailing, and the menu board on the black panel loses definition.
grades.lesson: Any text built from blocks or pixels must be drawn on a dedicated glyph grid with consistent stroke width, at least one empty cell between letters, and a single foreground colour against a contrasting background. Check that it reads correctly at thumbnail size in every colour variant before shipping.

flaws: Preset 'Classic' renders pixel-identical to Defaults. It is a wasted preset that shows the buyer nothing new.
In the 'Tram' preset the awning stripes wash out to near-white and pale pink. The awning, a signature feature in the brief, almost vanishes against the lit hatch interior.
The menu board's pixel glyphs become ambiguous in the Tram and dark-brand renders, reading as stray 'E' and '∃' marks rather than a menu.
Every range knob at maximum only slightly lengthens the truck. Little useful variation is exposed, and the hatch-open toggle is never shown closed, so its closed state is unverified.
Wheels read as detached square blocks hanging below the chassis, with a visible gap, which looks less resolved than the rest of the body.
The 'A' in the pixel 'EAT' sign is borderline and can read as 'R' at small sizes.
grades.lesson: Every preset must be visibly distinct from the defaults. Any derived colour pair, such as the stripes or highlights generated from a user colour, must be contrast-checked against its own surroundings so a feature never washes out when the base colour changes.

flaws: The roof sign's pixel lettering is malformed at default size. The middle glyph renders as a broken 'A' with a stray centre pixel, so it reads as 'EÄT' or 'EiT' in the defaults, both presets, night, and both brand probes. It only reads cleanly as 'EAT' in the max render. The sign is the focal point of the asset, so this is a broken render, not a nitpick.
At defaults and in the presets, the awning's right end runs into the menu board, which leaves the board partly occluded and looking crowded instead of deliberately placed.
At maximum ranges the awning grows down over the serving hatch. The burger and counter items are half-hidden behind the stripes, and the hatch stops reading as an open window.
Dark brand probe: the near-black body swallows the voxel seams and the door and cab edge detail. The light-grey bumper and base strip stay unbranded and look pasted on against the black.
A small red tail-light block on the rear corner floats off the body silhouette in every render.
Only open-hatch states are shown. The hatch toggle and lights knob are untested for the closed or unlit day state, so their range can't be confirmed.
grades.lesson: When a pixel or voxel font is drawn on a grid that scales with a knob, design each glyph at the smallest grid size it will render at and check the word reads correctly at defaults. Don't let glyphs be resampled from a larger master, because snapping drops or adds stray pixels and turns letters into different characters.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A delivery van with a tall cargo box, a logo panel and rear doors. Footprint 5x2. Knobs: body colour, logo colour, length 4-6 m, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights

flaws: The 'stripes' livery is broken. The lower stripes run off the cargo box, across the bare chassis deck and float in the air toward the cab instead of ending at the box edge.

At max range the rear doors break apart. A yellow panel sticks up and intersects the top-left corner of the cargo box, one door is detached and skewed, and the rear end no longer reads as a door assembly.

The silhouette is odd at every setting. A grey flatbed gap exposes bare chassis between the cargo box and the cab. The cab is undersized, tucked behind and unrelated to the body colour, so the asset reads as a box on a flatbed rather than a delivery van.
The logo reads as a medical cross, not a parcel. In the Blossom Bakery preset and the light brand probe the van looks like an ambulance, which undermines the 'logo panel' purpose.
The 'Parcel Post' preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no value as a preset.
At defaults the cab stays off-white regardless of the body colour. In the dark brand probe it jumps to an unrelated purple, so cab colour control is unclear and inconsistent.
In the dark brand probe the black rear doors and body lose almost all edge definition, and the door panels flatten into one mass.
The rear step plate in body colour sticks out awkwardly past the bumper and reads like a stray part.
grades.lesson: Derive every decorative or attached sub-part (stripes, decals, doors, trims) from the current dimensions of the surface it belongs to, and clamp it to that surface. Render each choice option and each range extreme against the host geometry before submitting, because overflowing or intersecting parts are the most visible breakage.

flaws: Wheels are flat dark cubes with a white square that stick out past the body. They read as bumpers or support blocks, not wheels, so the van looks like it sits on crates in every render.
The cab is a cluster of small stacked boxes with a tiny window, and it is hard to read as a driver's cab. The front end looks unresolved next to the clean cargo box.

The 'stripes' livery turns the logo panel into a dark slot that reads like a window. The logo icon is crammed into its far-left end, and the stripes run into the rear wheel block with no clean termination.
In night mode the taillights glow amber instead of red. The rear doors go near-black and lose their detail.
In the light brand probe the cream logo panel almost disappears against the white body, so the panel structure is lost. Only the teal icon carries.
The logo panel is oversized and fills nearly the whole side at defaults and at max length. It reads more like a billboard than a van livery.
Scale against the brief's 5x2 footprint and town-shop.mjs cannot be verified from the renders. The length knob changes proportion only modestly.
grades.lesson: When simplifying an object into blocks, keep the parts that define it (wheels on a vehicle, doors on a building) recognisable as those parts at thumbnail size. Check the silhouette before refining livery and colour.

flaws: The cab is the weakest-reading part of the model. From this iso angle the side window shows a large flat dark-grey slab with no seat or dash detail, so the cab can look doorless or unfinished next to the well-detailed cargo box.
In the dark brand probe the logo panel is near-black on a near-black body. Only the thin grey frame separates them, so the panel loses its role as a brand surface.
In the light brand probe the cream body and beige doors sit close in value to the pale background and lean on outlines to read.
At night the rear red reflectors glow amber rather than red, which muddies the tail-light read.
In the stripes livery the logo shrinks into a small box tucked against the stripes, with floating text bars. It reads as busier and less resolved than the default panel livery.
The roof strips keep their size and spacing at maximum length instead of scaling with the cargo box. This is minor but noticeable.
grades.lesson: When a secondary surface such as a panel, badge or trim takes its colour from the body colour, derive it with a guaranteed minimum value contrast against the body. Then check it in both the lightest and darkest brand probes, so it never merges into the body.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A clock tower: square brick tower with a clock face on the front, a belfry and pointed roof. Footprint 4x4. Knobs: brick colour, roof colour, height 8-16 m, lights.

flaws: The clock face is the hero feature, and it reads as noise at preview size. The hour marks are scattered dark pixels, the hands barely separate from them, and the right-hand face shows horizontal stripe artifacts across the cream disc in every daylight render.

The framing auto-fits each variant, so apparent scale drifts. The footprint is visibly smaller in the max-height render and larger in the gabled render than at defaults. For a kit piece meant to match town-shop scale on the 6 m grid, the previews cannot be compared or trusted for scale.

Dark brand probe: the pale lavender roof with near-white highlights loses its silhouette against the light background, especially on the lit facet. The clock faces become saturated cyan, which reads as a screen rather than a clock.
Harbour preset: the pure saturated blue on the roof and clock backgrounds is garish next to the muted stone. It breaks the restrained palette of the other presets.
Gabled roof: the cross-gable geometry is confusing at the front corner. The finial pokes out of an ambiguous ridge junction, and the roof overhang looks oversized relative to the belfry.
The bell is almost invisible inside the belfry, so the belfry reads as an empty box at defaults.
grades.lesson: Design the focal detail for the size it will actually be seen at: check it in the final preview at real resolution and simplify it (fewer, bolder marks; no sub-pixel or sub-voxel detail that aliases into stripes) until it reads instantly. A noisy hero feature sinks an otherwise solid asset.

flaws: The clock dials are the hero element, but they are built as stair-stepped pixel circles with protruding tick blocks. Every other surface is clean, flat-shaded geometry, so the dials look like an aliased raster pasted onto vector work rather than a deliberate style.

The clock hands are crude and hard to read at the default render size. The two visible faces also appear to show different times (one an L-shaped pair of hands, the other a single vertical hand with an orange hub), which looks like a mistake rather than a design choice.

At maximum height the shaft gains only stacked rows of identical windows, with grey unlit ones scattered at random. The tower starts to read as an office block. The clock stage and belfry also look proportionally smaller, and the cream eave slab sticks out as a flat ledge beyond the narrower roof base.
With faces set to "front", the blank side of the clock stage is a featureless brick slab with no recess, panel or louvre. It looks like something was left unfinished rather than intentionally plain.
The night render's navy roof almost disappears against the dark background, so the silhouette above the belfry is lost.

Scale against the brief is unclear. A 4x4 footprint on a 6 m grid implies a much broader base than this slender tower on its thin plinth, and the tiny door makes the tower's real-world height hard to judge.
grades.lesson: Build the element the asset is named after (here the clock face) at the same geometric fidelity as the rest of the model. Check it at thumbnail size in every preset: a stair-stepped circle or illegible glyph on otherwise clean geometry reads as a rendering bug, not a style.

flaws: Saddle roof option is broken: the belfry's top brick beams poke up through the roof's lower edge and form a V across the slope. The roof never sits cleanly on the belfry, and it loses the cornice and pinnacles without anything replacing them, so the top looks unfinished.
With the saddle roof, the roof overhangs further on one side than the other. It reads as a mismatched mesh dropped on top, not part of the tower.

At maximum height the tower is stretched evenly from base to top, so the belfry and clock band look squashed against the long brick shaft. The middle of the tower is mostly empty brick broken only by thin windows.
At the tallest setting the bell is mostly hidden behind the belfry columns. The belfry opening then reads as a dark empty void.
The ground-level lamp beside the door is a tiny yellow speck at default lighting and is easy to mistake for a rendering artefact.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob swaps in one part, such as a roof, make the new part sit exactly on the same mounting outline as the original, with matching overhang on every side. Then render each option on its own and check that no nearby part pokes through it.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bicycle leaning on a stand, made of thin boxes and two wheel rings approximated with 8 thin boxes each. Footprint 2x1. Knobs: frame colour, basket toggle.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights
colour knobs without a brand role: saddle

flaws: The object does not read as a bicycle at defaults. The two wheels render as square, ladder-like rectangular frames, not rings. The '8 thin boxes' approximation collapses into a box outline at this scale and angle.
The frame tubes are heavily stair-stepped voxel diagonals that look like green staircases rather than tubes. The top tube, down tube and seat tube merge into a cluttered tangle.
The grey and navy wheel and stand geometry overlaps the frame in confusing ways. It is unclear which parts are the wheels, the stand or the fork, and the silhouette is illegible.

Proportions are off. The basket and handlebar float high above a frame that sits low between the wheel squares. The bike also occupies only a small part of an oversized white slab, which wastes the 2x1 footprint.
The 'Tram' preset is pixel-identical to defaults, so it is a dead preset.
The 'every range knob at maximum' render is nearly indistinguishable from defaults, so the range knobs are barely doing anything perceptible.
The 'racer' style detaches parts. The handlebar and basket shift forward and float disconnected from the frame and head tube, which reads as broken assembly.
The basket toggle (a briefed knob) is never shown off in any render. Instead an unbriefed 'style' choice was added that breaks the model.
The brand probes recolour the saddle and grips to brand colours (bright purple, coral), which looks garish on a town-kit prop. The pinkish basket contents stay unchanged and visually noisy.
Night mode turns the slab a flat mid-grey that dominates the scene. The frame loses contrast against the dark wheels and becomes even harder to read.
grades.lesson: Before adding knobs, verify that the primitive approximation actually reads as the intended object at the kit's real render scale and camera angle. If a circle made of N boxes reads as a square, increase the segment count or change the representation, because silhouette legibility at defaults outranks every other feature.

flaws: The silhouette does not read cleanly as a bicycle at the default view. The frame tubes are dense stair-stepped voxel runs that look jagged and noisy rather than like thin tubes, and the down tube and seat tube merge into a messy V.

The wheels are not legible rings. The near wheel shows a chunky stepped arc on its upper-left and a dark lower arc, and its right side is lost behind the frame and stand. The far wheel is mostly hidden behind the basket. Neither reads as a closed wheel.

The tyre colour is split. Its upper arc takes a tint from the frame colour (pale green, cream, pink, pale lime), while its lower arc stays dark rubber. It looks like a material-assignment bug, not a design choice.
The grey stand rail runs parallel to the top tube and through the saddle area, so it visually fuses with the frame. It is hard to tell what is bike and what is stand.
The bike overhangs the 2x1 base plate. The rear wheel pokes past the left edge, so it will collide with neighbouring kit pieces on the 6 m grid.

The brand probes push the accent colour onto the saddle and grips. This gives a salmon-pink saddle in the light probe and a lavender saddle with lime frame in the dark probe. The result is garish, and the lime frame has poor contrast against the light ground.
Step-through is barely distinguishable from the default diamond frame at this scale, so the choice knob delivers almost no visible value.
At max range the model shifts on the plate and a loose grey kickstand block appears on the ground. The composition changes rather than scaling gracefully.
The brief asked for wheel rings made of 8 thin boxes each. The render instead uses many small stepped cubes, which is the cause of the noisy, heavy look.
grades.lesson: Check the silhouette at thumbnail size before adding detail. Build curved and diagonal members from a few rotated primitives rather than voxel staircases, keep fixed material roles (rubber, metal, wood) independent of the brand or accent colour, and keep the whole model inside its declared footprint.

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to the defaults. Either the range knobs do nothing or their maximum equals the default. In both cases the exposed range adds no value.

The brief asks for a bicycle leaning on a stand, but the bike stands perfectly upright in every render, including the kickstand variant. That variant swaps the block for a grey plate but leaves the bike vertical, so nothing about the pose changes.
The default 'stand' is an unexplained grey pillar and box under the bottom bracket. It reads as a modelling artefact rather than a bike stand.
The thin diagonal frame tubes render with a dense zipper or hatch pattern in every view. It looks like aliasing or a z-fighting texture, not a clean painted tube.
The wheel rings are chunky, near-square octagons with visible stepped notches where the 8 boxes meet. At this size they read more as square frames than wheels.
In the night render the navy tyres sit on a near-identical navy background. Both wheels almost disappear and the silhouette breaks down.
The lamp sits at the seat/top-tube junction rather than at the front or rear. It is an odd placement that a designer would notice.
The basket toggle named in the brief is never shown off. There is no basket-free render to confirm the bike still composes without it.
grades.lesson: Before submitting, render each range knob at its minimum and maximum and diff against the defaults; any knob that produces no visible change should be fixed or removed, because a dead knob signals an unfinished asset.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. An octagonal park gazebo with posts, a railing and a pointed roof (cone). Footprint 4x4. Knobs: post colour, roof colour, size.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: finial, lights

flaws: Faceted roof shading pushes the lit facets toward white. In the dark brand probe the lime roof's right facets are near-white and the eave silhouette almost vanishes. The tiered lower skirt is washed-out pink with weak facet separation. The cyan facet in the light brand probe is close to blowing out too.
Small pale wedge shapes poke past the main roof silhouette at upper left and upper right of the cone in the defaults. This reads as stray back-face or eave geometry and is visible at thumbnail size.

At 'every range knob at maximum' the footprint and post height barely change and the roof just gets taller. Above the eave there is a short vertical band before the slope, so it reads as a can-and-cone rather than a scaled-up gazebo. A designer setting 'size' would not get what they expect.
Preset 'Park' renders pixel-identical to the defaults, and 'Tram' only swaps the roof to green. The presets add no real value.
The finial changes to bright cyan in the dark brand probe, unrelated to the roof or post colour. That reads as an accident rather than intentional brand mapping.
At night the posts, railing and deck collapse into one muddy grey-mauve. The railing detail is lost and only the lanterns read.
grades.lesson: Derive face shading by darkening or multiplying from the input colour rather than lightening toward white, clamp lightness so every face keeps visible contrast against its neighbours and the background, and always test with a very light, very saturated hue (e.g. lime or cyan) as well as a dark one.

flaws: Tiered roof variant: the lower tier's lit faces wash out to near-white pink. It no longer reads as the same roof material as the saturated upper tier, and the arbitrary yellow band between tiers looks like a leftover accent rather than a designed trim.

Dark brand probe: the brand colour lands on the roof as a bright lime, and the railings repeat the same lime. The lit roof faces blow out to pastel and the piece looks garish rather than dark-branded. The probe does not show the asset adapting sensibly to a dark brand.

The plinth and steps are pale grey on the pale background with only hairline edges. The base reads as a ghost outline, and the gazebo looks like it floats rather than sitting on a solid footing, which weakens it as a ground-level kit piece.

Lanterns hang only on two right-hand posts at awkward heights. The front one overlaps its post silhouette and adds clutter instead of reading as deliberate entry lighting. The tiny lights under the eaves are barely legible at defaults.

The 'size' knob at maximum mostly stretches height and roof pitch. The proportions shift (the taller roof looks top-heavy) without a clear designer-meaningful outcome. There is no control for railing colour, which is silently tied to the roof colour.
The brief asked for post colour, roof colour and size. The extra roofStyle choice is welcome, but its only alternative is the weakest render in the set.
grades.lesson: Compute face shading as bounded, clamped lightness offsets in a perceptual colour space (e.g. OKLCH ±L with a max-L cap) rather than mixing toward white/black, and test with both very light and very saturated input colours. Otherwise lit faces and derived secondary surfaces wash out and lose the material's identity under arbitrary brand colours.

flaws: The size knob at its maximum is nearly identical to the defaults. The roof and plinth grow by a few pixels, so the 'every knob at max' render barely tests anything and the knob gives the designer almost nothing.
The tiered roof has a pale band between the lower and upper tiers. It reads as a gap with the upper tier floating rather than a deliberate vented drum.
The side railings are flat dark bars that run diagonally into and across the posts. Joints are unresolved and the railing looks pasted on rather than built between the posts.

In the dark brand probe the colours are mapped poorly: a lime roof, purple rails and a cyan finial clash. The brand colour lands on the rails while the roof takes an unrelated hue, so the piece does not read as on-brand.
The stair pad and lantern pillars push out past the octagonal plinth on one side. This risks breaking the stated 4x4 footprint and the clean octagonal silhouette the brief asks for.
Post caps sit right at the eave line and in places read as poking past the roof edge instead of tucking under a clear overhang.
At the default framing the asset fills only about a third of the canvas, so the detail (balusters, lantern caps) is too small to judge or use at thumbnail size.
