grades.lesson: Before shipping, render every range knob at its minimum and its maximum side by side. If the two extremes are not obviously different at thumbnail size, widen the range or cut the knob, because a knob that changes nothing visibly is a broken promise to the buyer.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A small arched footbridge 6x3 over water: deck boxes stepping up and down, railings. Knobs: wood colour, rail colour, water toggle.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights
colour knobs without a brand role: wood

flaws: The lily pad sits right on the water/bank boundary at the front corner and reads as half-overlapping the bank in every render, including night. It needs clear placement inside the water.
A thin beige stroke runs along the front edge of the left bank. It reads as a stray outline rather than a deliberate curb.
At the max-range extreme, the longer, taller bridge crowds the base. The left grass corner disappears and the landing nearly reaches the tile edge, so the piece feels cramped on the 6 m footprint.
Railing top rails follow the arch in straight segments with visible kinks. The stepped deck reads more like a staircase than an arch at defaults.
In both brand probes the brand primary lands on the deck, so it stops reading as timber and looks like plastic blocks. The dark-brand lime/violet pairing is harsh, but nothing is clipped.
The water toggle requested in the brief is not shown in any render, so it cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: Keep small decorative props a clear margin inside the zone they belong to (water, grass, deck) and never centred on a boundary between zones, so they cannot appear to straddle or clip into neighbouring surfaces at any size.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A windmill with a tapered tower, cap and four sails made of thin boxes. Footprint 4x4. Knobs: tower colour, sail colour, height, sail angle.

flaws: The sails clip through the roof cap in every render. The hub sits on the roof plane with no forward offset, so the upper sail lattice passes through the gable and dome caps.

The default gable cap reads as a flat tilted slab perched off-centre on an octagonal tower. It overhangs on one side, does not seat on the tower top, and looks unfinished next to the much better dome option.
At the maximum sail angle the rotated sails pierce the cap and become a noisy tangle of overlapping frames. The four-sail silhouette stops reading as a windmill.
The small crate at the base hangs half off the plinth ring beside the door step. It looks like a placement error rather than intentional dressing.
The tall, thin tower barely uses the 4x4 footprint. The plinth ring and door step are the only things that fill the footprint, so the piece feels undersized against a block kit's ground grid.
The 'Classic' preset renders identically to defaults, so it adds no value as a preset.
The dark brand probe pushes the sails to saturated lime on a near-black tower. Sail colour has no tonal guard, so the result is garish and fights the warm lit windows.
Window treatment is inconsistent: one mid-tier window is a grey-blue unlit pane while the others glow. It reads as a missing texture rather than a deliberate variation.
grades.lesson: Any rotating or protruding sub-assembly (sails, blades, signs) must be offset from the body along its axis by at least its own thickness plus clearance. Check that offset at every value of its rotation knob so it never interpenetrates other geometry.

flaws: The gable cap option is off-centre on the octagonal tower. The roof ridge sits shifted left of the tower axis and overhangs one side, so the cap looks dropped on rather than fitted.
At maximum sail angle the sails become a cramped cluster of chunky crosses that crowd and visually collide with the cap. They no longer read as four clean sails made of thin boxes.
At defaults the upper-left sail crosses in front of the top tower window. The front gallery post also stands directly in front of the door and crate, so the entrance is cluttered and partly occluded.
The door assembly reads as a freestanding slab in front of the tower base rather than an opening in the tower.
The brief asks for a tapered tower, but the result is a stepped octagon with no real taper.
The gallery deck with legs dominates the base and is not in the brief. Its posts make the 4x4 footprint read busy.
The dark brand probe produces lime-green sails against a blue cap, which looks garish. Colour mapping is not constrained to stay in the town palette.
The knob set covers the brief, but the sail angle range goes far enough to produce degenerate overlaps. There is no option to hide the gallery, which designers would want.
grades.lesson: Derive attachment points and clearances from the actual dimensions of the parent part, such as the tower axis, cap radius, and door and window positions. Then check every swapped or extreme-valued component against them, so that alternates stay centred and moving parts never cross key features.

flaws: At max, the sail lattice turns into a dense, aliased hatch of brown and red slats. It reads as noise rather than sail frames, and is effectively broken at that extreme.

Thin pale lines run outside the tower silhouette from cap to platform. They are faint at defaults and clearly visible in Polder and the dark brand probe. They look like a stray outer shell or misaligned edge geometry.
The protruding window boxes on the tapered tower sit like cubes pasted onto a sloped face and don't seat into the wall. They multiply at max height and look cluttered.
The sail lattice does not scale with tower height. At max the sails look undersized and spindly for the taller tower.
The asset occupies well under half the frame and leaves large dead space above. Weak presentation at defaults, even for a kit piece.
The brand colour drives both cap and sails, so there is no independent cap/roof control. The dark brand probe yields a muddy brown cap with weak contrast against the grey tower.
The base reads ambiguously. The tower stands on a flat slab supported by posts over a small annex, which feels like a porch roof rather than a mill foundation.
grades.lesson: Cap the count of repeated fine detail (slats, lattices, bands) as a function of the element's rendered size, so each sub-element stays several pixels wide at every knob extreme instead of collapsing into moiré.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A canal tile 6x6 with stone banks, water and a moored small boat. Knobs: stone colour, water colour, boat colour, boat toggle.

warnings: colour knobs without a brand role: stone, water

flaws: The 'small boat' reads as a cottage, not a boat. A gabled house with windows sits on the canal edge with no visible hull under it.
The boat is broken apart. The cabin overlaps the stone bank wall, while a long thin white and maroon sliver, apparently the hull, floats detached in mid-canal.
In the all-knobs-max render the hull sliver disappears entirely. The cabin sits half on the bank and half on the water, clipping into the quay wall.
The Harbour preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it is a dead preset.

In both brand probes the boat roof takes the same colour as the water. In the light probe it is teal on teal, and in the dark probe it is lime on lime, so the boat vanishes into the canal and boat colour is not independently respected.
The dark brand probe is garish and unusable. Fluorescent lime water against near-black banks makes the stone side walls illegible and kills the depth cues.
The stone bank side walls are barely distinguishable from the top surfaces in several renders, so the tile edges read flat.
The tile carries unrequested props (tree planter, bench, two lamps, sign) that a kit tile should leave optional. They crowd the composition and pin a scene onto what should be a neutral grid piece.
The front lamp post's base sits right at the water edge and reads as standing in the canal from this angle.
grades.lesson: Build compound props such as a boat with cabin and hull as one group positioned from a shared origin, and constrain it to its allowed region (e.g. inside the water, clear of bank walls). Then check every preset, extreme and brand render to confirm the parts stay attached, stay inside that region, and keep a colour distinct from the surface they sit on.

flaws: Light brand probe: the boat hull turns pale cyan on cyan water and nearly disappears. The hero object loses its silhouette, and only the brown deck reads.
Light brand probe: the bank tops go near-white on the light grey canvas with almost no edge definition, so the top surfaces bleed into the background.

At the far end of the channel there is a small fragment cut off by the tile edge. It takes the boat colour in every render (red, yellow, pink, cyan, lime). It reads as a clipped sliver of a second boat or an unreadable gate, not an intentional detail.
Promenade dressing: the green shrub on the left bank is crammed against the coping strip and partly hidden behind it. It looks half-buried rather than placed.

Night mode: the stone and boat darken, but the water stays a saturated mid-blue that reads like daytime. The lamps glow but cast no light on the scene, so the night state looks like a filter rather than a lighting change.
The max-range render barely differs from the defaults (slightly longer boat, nudged lamps). The range knobs offer little real variation for a tile meant to be reused across a town.
The brief asks for a boat toggle, but no boat-off render is shown, so the empty-canal state is unverified.
grades.lesson: When several elements derive their colours from the same brand input (e.g. boat and water), enforce a minimum luminance contrast between adjacent elements after derivation, and fall back to a lighter or darker shift when the contrast is too low. Otherwise the focal object vanishes in some brand palettes.

flaws: Light brand probe: the boat and the water both take the brand teal. The boat, the tile's focal object, nearly disappears into the canal.
Dark brand probe: the acid-lime boat on mint water reads as garish rather than intentional. Brand colour is applied raw with no tonal adjustment.
Mooring rope is not tied to the bollard. It starts on the wall lip or wall face below the bollard, and at max wall height the gap widens until the rope comes straight out of the masonry.
Lamp-reflection dashes on the water sit far from both lamps, near the right bank corner. At max range they spill over the right bank's face and read as stray artifacts rather than reflections.
The far lamp's pole ends exactly at the back edge of the bank with no visible base. It appears to stand behind or off the tile, which breaks clean tiling on a 6 m grid kit.
Promenade dressing: the rear planter is mostly hidden behind the far bank edge, showing only a sliver of green. It is either clipped or placed outside the footprint.
The left bank has brick coursing and a coping band, but the right bank is a blank slab. The asymmetry looks unfinished rather than designed.
No visible response of the water or boat to max wall height. The boat sits at the same apparent float level, so the deeper canal reads as a bigger box rather than a lower waterline.
grades.lesson: When brand colours drive several roles at once, derive a guaranteed contrast between a figure and the ground it sits on (boat vs water, text vs fill), e.g. by offsetting lightness or using a complementary role. Then verify the figure stays legible in every brand probe, not just the default palette.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A clipped hedge run with a gate gap option. Footprint 6x1. Knobs: leaf colour, height 0.6-1.8 m, gate toggle.

warnings: colour knobs without a brand role: leaf, bloom

flaws: The hedge does not read as a hedge. Each block is a hard-edged box with a stepped cap and inset rectangular panels on its faces, so the run looks like utility cabinets, lockers or mailbox banks rather than clipped foliage. The brand probes make this worse: the teal and lime versions read as dumpsters or vending units.
The 'scalloped' style stacks faceted octagonal drums on the boxes. It reads as pots or machinery, not a scalloped topiary profile.

At maximum height the gate and the left post do not scale with the hedge. The short picket gate sits in a tall canyon and the left post is lower than the hedge it should anchor, so the gate opening looks unconsidered.
The Spring preset renders identically to the defaults, so it adds nothing.
The Night render promises glowing lit parts, but nothing visibly glows. The pink and blue flower cubes and the gate hardware are as flat as everything else.
In the dark brand probe, the near-white top faces on the lime hedge wash out. The inset panels and segment breaks lose almost all contrast, leaving a flat neon slab.
The flower accents are uniform cubes stuck to faces at regular spots. They read as stickers or indicator lights rather than blossoms.
grades.lesson: Before adding surface detail, check at thumbnail size that the object still reads as its named material. Generic box-modelling moves like recessed panels and stepped caps make organic subjects look manufactured, so use irregular silhouettes, rounded or lumpy masses and broken edges for anything that grows.

flaws: The hedge does not read as clipped hedge. It reads as stacked, slightly offset boxes, with plain flat faces and arbitrary step seams on top.

Unexplained clutter is scattered across the piece: pink/white/cyan cubes and orange dots on the hedge tops, plus green rectangular panels lying on the white paving slabs. A designer cannot tell whether these are flowers, signs, planters or lights, and they add noise rather than meaning.

The gate does not sit cleanly in its opening. The picket leaf is narrower than the gap between the posts, it is not visibly hinged to either post, and it looks parked in the opening rather than fitted. The left post is half-swallowed by the hedge.

At maximum height a crossbeam/arch appears unannounced. The left lantern ends up perched on the beam end, and the low picket gate looks undersized against the 1.8 m hedge. New green panels with pink squares also appear stuck to the hedge faces.
The 'wild' style fragments the silhouette into floating, misaligned lumps with cube sprouts. The front-left mass overhangs its slab edge. It reads as broken geometry rather than an untrimmed hedge.
In the night render the scattered hedge-top dots glow brighter than the lanterns, which barely register. This inverts the obvious light hierarchy.

Knob behaviour leaks beyond the brief: height also adds an arch, and an undocumented 'style' choice exists. Height changing structure rather than only scale makes the kit piece unpredictable on the 6 m grid.
grades.lesson: Every visible element must be identifiable at a glance and tied to a named knob. Delete decorative bits that cannot be named, and never let a scalar knob like height silently add or remove structures.

flaws: A large, featureless white slab fills the right half in front of the hedge. It appears raised and hides the base of the right hedge. It reads as missing material or a stray filler plane, and it makes the piece lopsided against the planted bed on the left.
The hedge has a pitched, gabled top with pentagonal end faces, so it reads as a long shed or building rather than a clipped hedge. Clipped town hedges are flat-topped or softly rounded.
The gate's horizontal rails stick out past the pickets on the open side in every render. It looks like a modelling error, not a hinged gate.

Gate colour shifts with presets and brand probes to saturated blue, purple and orange-red. A garden gate in raw brand accent looks garish and does not fit a cohesive town palette. Copper Beech's green gate and Boxwood's electric blue clash with the foliage.
The dark brand probe turns the hedge acid lime and the flowers cyan, which is unnatural and cheap-looking. Leaf colour is not clamped to a plausible foliage range.
At maximum height the hedge towers over the gate pillars, so the gateway looks undersized. Pillar height should scale with hedge height.
The brief asks for a 6x1 footprint. The deep white apron makes the piece read deeper than one tile, and the asset will not tile cleanly as a hedge run.
Three knobs are as briefed, but the colour mapping bleeds into the gate and flowers. The gate-off state is not shown, so the toggle cannot be judged.
grades.lesson: Before shipping a block-kit piece, check every mesh against the briefed footprint and ground plane. Any surface without a clear material role (blank slabs, filler planes, oversized aprons) reads as a broken render, and it also breaks tiling with neighbouring pieces.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A rooftop or ground billboard on legs with a bold panel and lamps. Footprint 4x1. Knobs: panel colour, accent colour, height, lights.

flaws: Preset 'Sky' renders pixel-identical to the defaults, so it is a dead preset that gives the buyer nothing new.

The left edge of the panel has messy stacked geometry: the frame, the leg and stepped blue backing slabs overlap, and the slab tops show behind the bars. It reads as a modelling error, not a design choice.
The panel art is cluttered rather than 'bold'. The white chevron/'E' stack on the right is an ambiguous jumble of boxes, and in 'block' mode the white stack looks randomly piled and overlapping.

In the dark brand probe the whole structure turns near-white on a light background. The lamps become white-on-white and almost invisible, and the lime panel against cyan bars is garish and low-contrast. This probe is effectively broken.
In the light brand probe the panel and frame take the same teal, so the board loses its silhouette and reads as one flat mass.
The Night mode barely sells 'lit'. Only the two small lamps brighten, the panel receives no light wash, and the whites just go grey.
The lamps are tiny undifferentiated boxes sitting on the ledge with no fixture or arm. They hardly register as lamps at the defaults.

At the maximum knob settings the billboard is auto-framed so small that the panel shrinks to a minor element on very tall legs. The proportions become spindly and do not read like a scaled kit piece on the 6 m grid.
grades.lesson: When mapping brand colours onto a model, derive the structural and secondary parts from the brand colour with an enforced minimum contrast against both the scene background and the neighbouring parts. Then render light and dark brand probes and check that every small feature, such as lamps and trims, is still visible before shipping.

flaws: Structure does not hold together. The catwalk runs past the right edge of the panel with nothing under it. The right leg lands mid-catwalk rather than under the panel's right edge. The left post rises in front of the panel and reads as a separate column, so the frame is lopsided: heavy post on the left, nothing on the right.
The panel art is two arbitrary rectangles plus a white strip. It does not read as a bold billboard graphic, and at Night it fades to faint outlines, so the 'bold panel' in the brief is not delivered.
The lamp heads overlap the panel's top frame instead of hanging clearly off arms in front of it. At this size they read as blocks stuck to the panel.

The dark brand probe flips the frame from navy to light grey and the panel strip from white to near-black. That swaps the palette roles, so the model looks like a different asset. The lime-and-cyan result also clashes with the muted town-shop palette the brief asks for.
The height knob at maximum barely changes the silhouette. It adds a second brace and some leg length, but the panel proportion stays squat, so the range is too timid for rooftop versus ground use.
The 4x1 footprint is not clearly honoured. The panel looks narrower than the catwalk and the legs, so its grid alignment with town-shop pieces is doubtful.
grades.lesson: Derive every structural member (legs, posts, walkways, lamp arms) from the extents of the main panel, so that supports always sit under the edges they carry and nothing overhangs or floats at any knob value.

flaws: The panel's hero graphic is blocky pseudo-lettering that reads as 'ORS' / 'DRS' / 'DRE'. It looks like a misspelled or truncated word rather than a deliberate mark. A designer can't drop it into a town scene without it reading as a typo.
The lamp rig is inconsistent. There are three bracket arms on the panel top but only two lamp heads, both clustered left and centre. The right arm holds nothing, so it looks like a missing part.
In Night mode the effect is weak. The panel darkens instead of glowing, the lamps barely read as lit, and no light spills onto the panel face from the lamps. Most of the scene's appeal is lost.

In the Sunset preset the accent becomes off-white. The stripe on the grey walkway ledge nearly disappears, and Tram's pale pink is similarly faint. The accent colour isn't checked against the ledge surface it sits on.
The walkway ledge overhangs past the panel's right edge but stops flush on the left. This reads as an alignment slip, not a designed overhang.
The 'bars' art option is serviceable but thin. Two plain rectangles on a baseline give a designer little reason to choose it.
Positives: the dark brand probe correctly flips the glyphs to dark for contrast, the max-height variant adds crossbars sensibly, and nothing clips or breaks.
The asset is clean and on-palette for the kit, but the hero graphic and the half-populated lamp rig keep it below a paid-asset bar.
grades.lesson: Never put near-letterforms on a hero surface. Either render a real, legible word (or a user-editable text knob), or use clearly abstract graphics, because shapes that almost read as letters look like a typo and undermine the whole asset.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A playground with a slide, swings frame and a sandbox on a soft mat. Footprint 6x6. Knobs: mat colour, slide colour, swings 1-3, sandbox toggle.

flaws: The soft mat covers only the front half of the 6x6 footprint. The back half is bare white plinth, and the swings frame and slide tower stand on nothing. It reads as unfinished, not as a playground on a soft mat.
Mat tiles are a patchwork of two greens laid unevenly, with gaps and edges that do not align to the grid. This looks careless next to a clean kit piece.
The slide tower sits jammed against the back-right edge. Its brown base appears cut off where it meets the plot, and the slide runs to the plot edge. At max it pokes slightly past the edge.
The swings frame shows hanging chains but only one visible seat. Other chains end in empty air, so it is unclear whether the swing count knob actually adds seats.
At max range the enlarged slide and the dark-red tower overlap into a muddy red mass, and the roof looks perched rather than attached.
The Night render claims lit parts glow, but nothing glows. It is a uniform darkening, and the white plinth turns a dull lavender-grey.
In the light brand probe, the beige mat on a white plinth is very low contrast, and the composition washes out.
The sandbox's floating red bucket and loose tile square sit on the mat with no clear relation to anything.
The brief asks for a sandbox toggle and swings 1-3, but no render demonstrates either knob working. The max render changes only scale and shows no third seat.
grades.lesson: Before placing props, cover the entire footprint with the ground surface and lay props out against that full plot. Then check the render at a glance for large unintended empty areas or objects standing on bare base. An asset whose ground covers half its footprint reads as unfinished no matter how good the props are.

flaws: The swing frame's right A-frame legs pass through the bench at defaults. At max (3 swings) the wider frame swallows the bench almost entirely, which is a visible interpenetration.
A large dark-red triangular plane juts left from the slide tower under the platform. It reads as a broken or mis-wound slide side wall, not intentional geometry.
The yellow spring rider sits jammed against or into the base of the slide ladder, with no clearance between the two items.
The sandbox's front wall crowds or overhangs the mat's white rim, so it does not sit cleanly inside the 6x6 footprint.

The max-knob render changes the overall plot scale and object positions: the tower is taller, the lamp moves and the plot is larger. A fixed 6 m-grid kit piece must keep an identical footprint so it tiles with town-shop.
Preset 'Park' is pixel-identical to Defaults, so it is a wasted preset.
Swing chains and seats are thin, low-contrast strokes that nearly vanish at this render size, especially in the Night render.
Brand probes and the Night render otherwise recolour sensibly, and the lamp glow works, but this does not offset the collision problems.
grades.lesson: Lay out every sub-object in a kit piece against reserved footprint cells with clearance, and re-run a collision/bounds check at every count-knob value, so that growing one element (e.g. more swings) can never push it into a neighbour or off the fixed tile footprint.

flaws: At swings=3, the widened swing frame drives straight through the bench. The right post and crossbar visibly intersect it, a hard collision in a render the knob range is supposed to support.
The swing frame grows toward the play tower instead of into open mat space, even though the left edge of the mat has room. The layout does not reserve clearance for the knob's maximum.
In every render, the front row of mat tiles steps forward past the white plinth rim. Their darker side faces sit outside the base edge, so the mat reads as misregistered with its footprint.

The slide reads as a solid filled wedge or tent, not a chute. A flat red panel also spreads left under the tower deck, so the play structure's silhouette is muddy and the slide is hard to identify at a glance.
The bench is jammed against the tower's base with no breathing room, even at defaults, so the left half of the composition feels crowded while the right half is mostly empty mat.
The sandbox toggle is never shown in its off state, so it cannot be verified that the mat looks intentional without the sandbox.

Presets recolour the swing and tower frame, but the brief's knob list exposes no frame-colour control. The brand probes show this matters (purple on lime is harsh), so the knob set and the presets are inconsistent.
grades.lesson: When a count or size knob makes a part grow, give that part a reserved footprint sized for the knob's maximum, or grow it toward open space. Then render the max before shipping and check that it never intersects neighbouring props.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A flower cart with wheels and buckets of colourful flowers. Footprint 2x1.5. Knobs: cart colour, flower colours seed, buckets 3-8.

flaws: The cart does not read as a flower cart. Large grey buckets dominate the silhouette, and each holds only one or two small, sparse flower forms. At town-kit viewing distance it reads as a cart of metal pots.

Flower geometry is too abstract to identify. The pink spikes, purple cube clusters and flat orange squares do not read as blooms. The faceted red dome, which turns purple at max, looks like a jar lid or gemstone rather than a flower.
At max buckets the red cone flowers crowd up against the front awning post and underside, and appear to intersect them. There is no clearance logic between flower height and the canopy.
The front signboard carries a small red plus or cross on a cream panel. This reads as a first-aid or pharmacy mark, which is wrong semantics for a flower vendor.
In the Night render, nothing visibly glows despite the 'lit parts glow' mode. The scene is only darkened, so the night variant adds nothing.
grades.lesson: Make the brief's defining content the visual hero. Give it more volume, colour mass and recognisable form than its containers and supports, and check that the object is identifiable from silhouette alone at the kit's normal viewing distance.

flaws: The 'pots' choice knob set to 'enamel' renders effectively identical to the default. The buckets stay the same grey, so it is a dead knob at render scale.
The front buckets interpenetrate the cart: their grey bodies poke down through the front rim and side rail, and the left yellow bunch overlaps the awning post.
The hanging lantern at the back intersects the orange flower bucket in every render with the awning. It reads as a collision, not a placement.
The Blossom preset washes the awning out to white on white. The stripe pattern that defines the silhouette nearly disappears, and the pink edge is the only accent.
The brief's 'buckets 3-8' is hard to read across renders. The max render changes flower species and colours far more visibly than bucket count, so the count knob is not clearly expressed.
The rear wheel is mostly hidden behind the body, which makes the cart look one-wheeled and lopsided from this camera angle.
grades.lesson: Before shipping, render each option of every choice knob next to the default and diff them; if an option does not produce a clearly visible change at thumbnail size, either make it visibly distinct or remove it.

flaws: The front-left corner is crowded. The lantern, post and nearest bucket stack on top of each other, so the corner reads as a tangle and the bucket silhouette is lost behind the lantern.
Wheel treads render as a jagged comb of stepped voxels. They look noisy next to the cleaner deck and awning blocks.
The pennants under the awning are tiny and cluttered. At this scale they read as visual noise more than detail.
In the 'top: none' render the cart keeps a back-only gantry with hanging bulbs. It works, but it reads as a leftover frame rather than a designed open-top variant.
The enamel pot blue is very saturated. It fights the flowers and the town palette, especially next to the green trim.
grades.lesson: When a prop has contents that can be added or moved (buckets, crates, items), keep a clear zone around fixed accessories like lanterns, posts and signs. That way no item count or layout ever lets them overlap or hide each other's silhouettes.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A pond tile 6x6: grass edge, water as a thin pale blue box, lily pads, reeds, a little wooden jetty. Knobs: water colour, lily pads 0-8, jetty toggle.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights
colour knobs without a brand role: water, grass, blossom

flaws: Lily pads render as half-discs in every render. They appear to intersect the water slab, so they read as sunk or clipped rather than floating.
The water is drawn as a tiled grid with strong lines, so it reads as a swimming pool or floor tiles rather than a pond surface.
The water box pokes out past the white coping at the front-left corner, leaving a visible blue sliver. This gets worse at max range, where a blue strip runs along the front edge beneath the coping.
The grass base has a visible seam or step near the front corner, where the slab looks like misaligned pieces rather than one tile.
A loose grey stone block sits on the grass edge at the front. At max range it collides with the coping corner stone.
Dark brand probe turns the water lime green and the grass purple. The pond no longer reads as water at all, and the lily pads and reeds lose contrast against the lime surface.
Light brand probe turns the grass saturated salmon/red-orange with a hot orange edge. It is garish, and the tile no longer reads as a grass edge.
The Meadow preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, and Lotus is only a slight water tint shift. The presets add no real range.
Max range scatters reeds into the open water and right up to the jetty, making the composition cluttered.
The brief asked for water colour, lily pads 0-8 and a jetty toggle. None of the renders show the jetty toggled off or lily pads at 0, so those ends of the knob range go unproven.
grades.lesson: Map brand colours onto accent and structural roles only, never onto materials whose identity depends on their hue (water, foliage, skin, sky). Let brand tint those materials within a bounded hue range instead, so the object still reads as itself under any brand.

flaws: Stray props sit on or over the tile perimeter in every render. Pink/orange flowers at the left and back edges and a grey box at the back-right corner hang half off the grass slab and read as glitches, not detail.
The jetty base collides with the white coping on the right edge, so the coping runs straight through the wooden block.
The thin jetty beam extends into the water at an odd angle with no visible support. It reads as a floating stick.
An orphan white slab sits on the grass to the right of the jetty with no clear purpose.
The coping only runs along the two front edges. On the back two sides the water meets the grass directly, so the pond looks unfinished from the hero angle.
At max, reeds spawn in the middle of the water and pierce through lily pads. A row of reed posts also lines the back grass edge, and one stands above the tile corner.
At max, reed density and placement look random, not composed, and the lily-pad cluster crowds into the reeds.
The 'Night (lit parts glow)' render shows no glowing elements. It is just a darker palette, so the advertised behaviour is missing.

The brand probes recolour the grass to pastel yellow or mint and push the water to saturated cyan. The light-brand grass reads as sand, and neither probe holds the town-kit palette the brief asks to match.
The brief specifies three knobs (water colour, lily pads 0-8, jetty toggle), but the range knobs also change reed count and jetty position. Prop placement is not constrained when knobs move.
grades.lesson: Give every scattered or count-driven prop an explicit footprint. Clamp placements inside the tile's walkable bounds, inset from the edge, and reject positions that intersect other props or fixed structures (coping, jetty, water vs. land). Then verify at maximum counts, because collisions and edge overhangs only become obvious when density is highest.

flaws: It reads as a swimming pool, not a pond. A crisp white coping surrounds the water and a regular tile grid is drawn across the water surface. The brief asked for a grass edge, and this treatment turns a natural feature into a built one.
A row of white tick marks sticks out of the front-left and front-right edges of the coping onto the grass. They look like broken geometry or z-fighting rather than a deliberate detail.
A tiny stray object sits alone on the grass at the far right corner. Its colour changes with the brand, but at this size it reads as debris.
The jetty's land end runs over the coping onto the grass at the right edge. It doesn't clearly rest on anything, so the joint looks unresolved.
Presets are barely distinguishable. Lotus is practically identical to defaults, and Dusk only slightly tints the water and accents. They add little value.
At the maximum render, the lily pad count looks like about 6, not the 8 the brief specifies, and some pads overlap each other.
Brand probes recolour only a few pixel-sized flower accents. The light and dark probes look almost the same, so brand colour has almost no presence in the asset.
Reeds at maximum become an evenly spaced fence along the back edge rather than a natural clump, which strengthens the man-made pool look.
grades.lesson: Before polishing, check that the render reads as the noun in the brief. Edge and surface cues like hard white coping and regular grid lines can flip a natural feature (a pond) into a different object (a pool). If the brief specifies an edge treatment such as grass, build exactly that, and keep geometric patterns off organic surfaces.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A carousel with a striped cone roof, central pole and blocky horses on poles. Footprint 6x6. Knobs: roof colours, horses 4-8, lights.

flaws: Dark brand probe: the base, rim and entrance step all turn white or pale grey on a pale canvas. The platform loses its silhouette and the step disappears. The lime/lavender roof reads as garish rather than branded, so the probe looks unmapped rather than intentional.
At max horses (8), the front-left horses crowd into each other and each other's poles. There is no clear spacing between figures, and the ring looks jammed rather than evenly distributed.
The 'Classic' preset is pixel-identical to defaults, so a preset slot is wasted.
The brief asks for a central pole, but at the default camera the canopy fully hides it. Only a squat drum is visible, so the carousel's core structure doesn't read.
The horses barely read as horses: heads and necks are ambiguous blocks, and the brown ones in particular look like generic quadrupeds or crates at kit scale.
Night mode drains the horses to flat grey. They lose all character while only the rim lights glow, and the interior goes muddy.
In the light brand probe, one lit roof panel blows out to near-white and breaks the stripe rhythm.
grades.lesson: When remapping an asset to an arbitrary brand palette, assign the grounding/structural surfaces (bases, rims, plinths) from the palette's darkest usable tone and enforce a minimum contrast against the canvas, so the silhouette never dissolves into the background regardless of which brand is applied.

flaws: The horses are the defining feature, but at the kit camera they read as indistinct grey/cream voxel clumps. Head, legs and body cannot be told apart, and the yellow or red saddle cube is the only legible part.
The roof eave hides the back half of the ring. Horses at the rear left and rear right only peek out as fragments under the overhang.
At max (8 horses) only about 6 are discernible, so the horses 4-8 knob barely changes the read.
Every range knob at maximum looks almost identical to the defaults. The knob ranges are too timid to give the designer real range.

Dark brand probe: the navy brand colour lands only on the base trim, and the roof uses a pale lime that is barely distinguishable from the white and lavender stripes. The roof stripes wash out, and the result does not read as a dark-brand variant.
In the dark brand probe, cyan saddles, lime roof and navy base produce an incoherent palette. Brand roles map to parts arbitrarily.
The entry steps protrude past the octagonal plinth edge at the front right. This risks breaking the 6x6 grid footprint when tiled against neighbouring kit pieces.
At night the horses and floor sink into near-identical muted greys. Only the roof bulbs and drum carry the image, and the horses disappear entirely.
The platform floor uses a noisy brown dirt texture that looks muddy next to the flat-shaded kit palette.
grades.lesson: The element that names the asset (here the horses) must be legible at the default camera and thumbnail size, and must not be hidden by other geometry. Scale it, simplify its silhouette and place it where the fixed camera can see it before adding anything else.

flaws: The horses are the hero element of a carousel, but they barely read as horses. At the rendered size they are white block clusters with dark leg stubs, with no clear head, neck or mane silhouette, and several are mostly hidden behind poles and the central drum.
The coloured saddle cubes (red/blue/green/magenta depending on palette) look like detached floating blocks beside the poles rather than parts of the horses, which adds visual noise near the centre.
At the max-range render the extra horses are hard to distinguish from the default count. The horses 4-8 knob produces little visible difference, so it reads as weak or broken.
The roof is tall at max, while the platform and horses stay the same size, so the piece becomes top-heavy. The horses shrink in visual importance, which makes them read even worse.
The kit piece occupies well under half the frame at defaults. That may be correct for 6 m grid scale, but the small details (horses, lights, drum) lose legibility at thumbnail size.
In the light brand probe, the dark platform skirt and the teal deck are low-contrast against each other. The tiered edge of the base turns muddy.
The night mode is the strongest render: the lit bulbs and glowing drum are attractive. The daytime presets, however, are mostly palette swaps of the same composition with no other variation.
grades.lesson: Make the asset's defining sub-element (here the horse) readable by silhouette alone at the final thumbnail size before polishing anything else. Exaggerate its key features (head, neck, ears) over literal voxel accuracy, and make sure any count knob produces a clearly visible change.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A small tram station platform 6x3 with a canopy, a bench, a clock and a sign. Knobs: canopy colour, sign colour, lights.

flaws: The clock face is illegible in every render. It reads as a garbled cluster of black pixel blocks on white, not a dial with hands, and the glyph changes shape between the flat and pitched renders. The clock is a required brief element and the focal point of the piece.
In Night, the sign glows as a flat yellow box and the 'T' glyph vanishes. The clock is also unreadable, so the lit state loses the two signage elements it is meant to highlight.
In the dark brand probe, the posts and frame turn near-white and dissolve against the white tile platform and pale background. The structure loses its silhouette.
The canopy front fascia renders in a much more saturated hue than the roof top, giving neon blue in Harbour and neon lime in the dark probe. Shading looks inconsistent with the rest of the kit.
The 'Tram Green' preset is identical to the defaults, so it adds no range.

At max, the canopy lengthens while the platform keeps its 6x3 footprint. The left end overhangs the platform edge, and the clock and sign stay put while the canopy and bench shift, so they look unanchored and the piece drifts off the 6 m grid the brief requires.
There is no direct sign colour knob. The sign recolours only as a side effect of presets and brand probes, and in the dark probe it shifts to cyan.
grades.lesson: Check small detail elements at the actual delivered render size, in day, night and both brand probes. These include clock faces, glyphs and icons. If they don't read, reduce them to a few bold primitives with fixed contrast against their own backing panel.

flaws: A lighter, off-colour patch sits on the front-left corner of the roof, next to the fascia. It appears in every render: defaults, Harbour, Terracotta and both brand probes. It looks like geometry from below (the side panel, frame or light strip) poking through the canopy, or coplanar faces z-fighting. It reads as a defect.

The dark brand probe renders as a bright lime roof with a saturated cyan sign and a neutral grey frame. It does not read as a dark brand, and the lime/cyan pairing is garish. Brand colour mapping looks wrong or unguarded.
At every range knob's maximum, the sign and post crowd into the front-left glass panel and visually overlap its edge. A stray small dark element floats above the sign.
At maximum knobs and with the pitched roof, a pale gap opens between the left side panel and the canopy. It looks like a missing infill piece, not a deliberate glazing detail.
At maximum knobs, the canopy grows while the platform stays the same size. The roof nearly reaches the platform edge, which breaks the 6x3 module proportions on the 6 m grid.
The clock face is a white square with an ambiguous L/J glyph and a red block. It does not read as a clock at kit scale.
The brief asked for canopy colour, sign colour and lights knobs. The extra range knobs mostly produce the broken states above instead of useful variation.
grades.lesson: Wherever two parts meet (panel tops under a roof, strips under a fascia), offset or trim one so it never shares a plane with or pokes through the other, then inspect every surface at defaults and at extremes for stray off-colour patches before submitting.

flaws: The clock is the focal detail and is not properly placed. It hangs below the front edge of the canopy with no visible bracket and overlaps the lit fascia strip, so it reads as floating in front of the canopy or clipping through it. This happens in every render, including the pitched-roof variant.
The clock face has a stair-stepped, aliased outline. Every other part of the model is smooth and flat-shaded, so the clock looks like a pasted-in sprite rather than part of the same kit.
The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to the defaults, so numeric knobs either do not exist or do nothing. The only real variation comes from colour, lights and the roof choice.
In the dark brand probe the canopy becomes a pale, washed-out sage. A dark brand produces a light, low-contrast canopy against the white platform, which suggests the brand colour mapping is wrong.

The shelter has a single glass end panel and only a thin back post. The front-right corner of the canopy looks unsupported, and the bench is barely covered. The model reads as an unfinished structure rather than a convincing tram stop.
In the pitched-roof variant the glass panel no longer meets the roof eave, leaving a gap that the flat-roof version hides.
grades.lesson: Every mounted or hanging element must visibly attach to something (bracket, rod or post) and must not intersect neighbouring geometry. Render every curved part at the same smoothness as the rest of the model so no single detail looks stair-stepped or pasted in.

brief: A wooden mug set down on a tavern table: fullness (empty to full of ale) choice, how hard it lands, table thickness, a slosh toggle; seeds change the wobble.

flaws: The impact body rings as sustained horizontal tonal lines for about 0.3 s, like a lightly damped metal or glass resonator. Wood on oak should be a dead, heavily damped thunk that decays in roughly 100 ms.
There is little broadband contact click at the onset. Most energy sits in the bottom third of the spectrogram, so the landing reads as soft and blurry rather than a crisp wood knock.

The fullness choice does not change the impact itself. Empty and full both have a centroid of about 615 Hz with the same body. Empty is visually identical to slosh=false (same 41% silence, same picture). An empty mug should sound hollower and brighter, and a full one heavier and duller.
The fullness choice and the slosh toggle overlap. Fullness only seems to gate the liquid layer, which duplicates the toggle and makes empty plus slosh meaningless.

The landing-force range is timid. Peak only moves from 0.50 to 0.76 and centroid from 656 to 773 Hz between the minimum and maximum renders. A gentle set-down versus a slammed mug should differ hugely in level and brightness.
The slosh layer appears as discrete late blips plus an odd rising diagonal tone around 0.4–0.5 s, rather than liquid motion that starts with the impact and settles.
Seeds read as takes of the same sound, which is fine, but the variation is mostly in the slosh tail rather than the wobble of the mug itself.
grades.lesson: Each control must change the core of the sound it names, not just switch a secondary layer on or off. Check that its extremes measurably shift the main event's spectrum and envelope, and that it does not duplicate another knob.

flaws: The slosh layer is unfiltered broadband noise. It smears evenly from the bottom to the top of the spectrogram and pulls the default centroid to about 2.75 kHz. Ale in a mug should be a low-mid gurgle and splash, but this reads as a hiss or shaker burst laid over the knock.

The wood impact itself is plausible. With slosh=false the knock has a centroid around 750 Hz, a short decay and some low resonant lines. At defaults, though, the noise layer swamps it, so the defaults do not sound like a wooden mug on oak.
At fullness=full the slosh bump around 0.2 s is as loud as the impact or louder. A mug being set down should not slosh harder than it lands.
At fullness=empty the slosh layer is still faintly present, as scattered noisy fragments in the mid-highs. An empty mug cannot slosh, so fullness should gate the slosh layer out.
The default fullness gives a centroid of 2754 Hz, higher than either extreme (about 1690 Hz at both empty and full). That means fullness is not a monotonic or interpretable control.
Every render is exactly 0.45 s regardless of hit force, fullness or table thickness. The duration appears hard-coded rather than following the physics.
grades.lesson: When adding a secondary layer such as liquid, debris or rattle, band-limit and shape its noise to the material. Also check that the layer stays subordinate to the main event, and that it disappears when the parameter that justifies it (here, fullness) goes to zero. Raw white noise layered on a physical impact almost always reads as hiss rather than as the material.

brief: Loopable 3 s steady downpour on asphalt and parked cars; knobs: surface (asphalt|concrete|mixed), rain density 0..1, drip detail 0..1, distance 0..1, loop crossfade toggle

flaws: The 'parked cars' part of the brief does not show up. The spectrogram has no tonal ping or resonance streaks from metal panels or roofs, just broadband wash with drip transients, so it reads as generic street rain.
Default centroid of about 1.2 kHz is a little dull for a close downpour on hard asphalt. It sounds slightly distant even before the distance knob is used.

Rain density at minimum still gives near-continuous noise (silence 2%). The low end reads as a lighter downpour rather than a sparse drizzle, so the density sweep is narrower than the 0..1 range suggests.
The crossfade on and off renders are almost identical. The loop seam cannot be checked from these renders, so the toggle's value is unproven.
Peak is pinned at 0.664 across nearly every render, which points to hard normalisation or limiting. That could flatten drip dynamics.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a specific sound source (e.g. 'on parked cars'), synthesise it as its own recognisable layer with a visible signature, such as tonal resonances or distinct impacts. Do not fold it into generic noise. Buyers pay for the named detail, and its absence makes the product generic.

brief: Car tire hits a deep puddle and throws a sheet of water; knobs: puddle size (small|medium|large), speed 0..1, curb slap 0..1, spray scatter 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: puddle=small is nearly indistinguishable from the medium default. It has the same envelope, the same ~1 s wash and the same tail, differing only by a slightly lower RMS (0.085 vs 0.097) and a slightly higher centroid. A designer choosing 'small' gets no audibly smaller splash.
Curb slap at maximum shows no distinct slap transient. The every-max render is a single, longer, brighter wash, so the knob seems to fold into general spray instead of adding its own event.

Low-frequency body is confined to the first ~100 ms. A tire punching into a deep puddle should carry more low-mid weight through the initial sheet. The wash above that is mostly mid/high noise, which reads closer to a thrown bucket than a vehicle.
The tail contains thin horizontal tonal streaks in the mids (sustained sine-like pings) that risk sounding synthetic against the noisy droplet ticks.
grades.lesson: When a knob offers discrete size choices, make each step change at least two structural features (duration, low-frequency weight, number or spacing of events), not just level or brightness, and check every option side by side so that no two read as the same sound.

flaws: At defaults this reads as a generic splash: a sharp impact burst, a ~0.8 s broadband decay, then sparse drip ticks. There is no swelling, sustained 'shhh' of a water sheet being thrown off a moving tire, and nothing in the envelope suggests a passing car.
39-47% silence at defaults and large puddle: much of the reported length is near-empty sparse droplets rather than spray mass.

The large puddle is mostly padded by a longer dead drip tail. Its main body is about the same length as at defaults and the centroid only drops slightly, so it doesn't sound like a bigger volume of water.
The small puddle shows two separated hits with narrow tonal low-frequency streaks. It reads as two slaps rather than a smaller splash.
All-maximum render has a stretch of horizontal tonal banding around 0.7-1.3 s, which sounds like buzzy resonant noise rather than water. It then ends fairly abruptly.
With the tail off, the sound is truncated: the waveform and spectrogram stop on a hard edge at about 0.8 s instead of decaying. This is a broken render.
Peak is pinned at 0.9 in every render. This looks like blanket normalization, so the hits won't keep their relative loudness when used together.
Knob list is reasonable, but the size choice doesn't scale the body and the speed knob shows no visible whoosh or rate character in the renders.
grades.lesson: When a size or intensity control is meant to make a sound 'bigger', scale the audible main body (duration, low-end mass, density) rather than appending sparse trailing events. Any toggle that removes a section must hand off with a short fade, never a hard cut.

flaws: At defaults the body is a smooth, uniformly broadband noise wash (flat speckle from bottom to top of the spectrogram for ~0.8 s). It has none of the granular, droplet-dense texture or low-mid water-mass 'slosh' that makes a tire-through-puddle read as liquid. It will likely sound like a filtered white-noise whoosh.
There is no impact moment. The onset is a soft ramp into the noise rather than a tire-meets-water hit, so the 'deep puddle' weight is missing.
The bottom of the spectrum is weak and undifferentiated. A deep puddle and a heavy tire should put clear energy and some motion in the low-mid region, but only a faint warmer band hugs the floor.
Curb slap is not visible as a distinct transient even with every range at its maximum, so the knob appears to do little or to be buried in the noise.
The drip tail is a handful of isolated identical ticks spaced across ~0.8 s (28% silence). It reads as sparse clicks rather than water falling back and pattering.
Small vs large mostly changes length and centroid. The character of the splash (mass, impact, spray density) does not change, so the sizes feel like time-stretches of one noise envelope.
The two seeds have the same envelope with only noise-level detail changing. That is acceptable, but the timing of the main spray mass and the onset hit do not vary.
grades.lesson: Liquid sounds are not shaped noise: build water from many short, pitched, randomly timed droplet/bubble events layered over a mass component, and make sure every control knob (like an impact or slap) produces a clearly visible transient in the render at its maximum.

brief: Short honk echoing down a wet block; knobs: horn type (compact|sedan|truck), length 0..1, distance 0..1, street echo 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Nearly every render is about half dead air: 48% silence at defaults and 46–51% on compact, truck, min and both seeds. The sound is over by roughly 0.9 s, and the file is padded with flat silence to 1.7–2.1 s. An editor would have to trim every instance.

No audible street echo. The tail is a smooth exponential smear, with no discrete slap-back or repeats along the block. Only the compact render shows faint stepping. 'Echoing down a block' is the headline of the brief, and it does not come through at defaults.
Nothing reads as 'wet'. There is no high-frequency tyre-hiss or rain-surface texture in any spectrogram. The ambience is just a dry horn plus decay.

horn = truck stops being a horn. The spectrogram is a broadband low noise wash with weak harmonics, where an air horn should show strong, clearly stacked harmonic lines. It reads as rumble or noise, not a tonal truck horn.

tail = false still shows a long decaying envelope (about 0.4 s of fade), so the toggle's effect is unclear. It actually produces a longer, denser body than the default. The difference from tail = true reads as a length change, not a tail removal.
Range at max gives a 1.2 s sustained honk. This is plausible, but combined with the trailing silence it makes the long end feel bloated rather than distinct.
grades.lesson: Trim the render buffer to the actual audible end (last sample above roughly −60 dB plus a short safety fade) instead of allocating a fixed or worst-case length. Large trailing silence is a defect buyers will notice immediately in every instance.

flaws: The horn is a single steady harmonic stack. Real car horns are usually a beating two-tone pair, and nothing here shows that dissonant interval, so it reads more like a synth tone or organ stab than a horn.

There is no visible 'echoing down a wet block': the tail is a smooth exponential fade, not discrete or smeared slap-back repeats off building faces. There is also no broadband wet-street component (tyre hiss or drip noise) in the spectrogram.

A thin full-height vertical line appears at the same position (about 0.15 s) in almost every render, including both seeds and tail=false. It looks like a broadband click or discontinuity artifact baked into the horn.
The tail toggle barely changes anything (1.28 s down to 1.04 s, same decaying envelope). It appears to duplicate the street echo knob rather than cleanly removing the reflections.

horn=compact differs from the default mainly in overall level and a slightly higher centroid (985 vs 871 Hz). The waveform turns into a dense block with similar harmonic spacing, so compact vs sedan is not clearly differentiated. Truck is the only choice with a clearly distinct character.
At all-maximum the sound runs 2.1 s with a lumpy double-swell envelope, which stretches 'short honk' into something closer to a held drone.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a spatial or acoustic effect (echo, room, distance), make it visibly distinct in the render: discrete or clearly smeared reflections, not just a longer fade. Also check every render for broadband vertical lines that signal clicks from unsmoothed parameter or envelope jumps.

flaws: A broadband click appears in almost every render. It shows as a thin full-height vertical line in the spectrogram around 0.2–0.25 s, partway through the honk, and lines up with a spike in the waveform. It is present at defaults, truck, every-range-minimum, every-range-maximum and both seeds. tail=false has extra clicks around 0.3 s and 0.55 s. This is a discontinuity, probably from a segment or pitch switch without a crossfade, and an editor cannot use a honk that ticks.
The compact render has stray vertical spikes in the last ~0.15 s of the tail, meaning clicks in what should be a clean fade.

At defaults, 'echoing down a wet block' reads as a smooth exponential decay, not discrete street slapbacks. Only the compact type shows separated repeats, so the echo character depends on horn type instead of the street echo knob.
Defaults carry 38% silence on a 1.31 s file. The usable honk plus decay ends around 0.9 s, leaving dead air the editor has to trim.
The wet-street layer (tyre hiss or rain wash) is barely visible: only faint scattered high-frequency specks. 'Wet' is not really sold.

The horn types differ mostly in harmonic density and fundamental. The truck honk is plausible as low and thick, but compact also changes the temporal pattern, which makes the horn type knob do two jobs.
grades.lesson: Whenever a synth switches segments, pitches, voices or envelope stages mid-sound, crossfade or ramp over a few milliseconds and zero-cross the edges. Then inspect every render's spectrogram for thin full-height vertical lines, which are clicks, before submitting.

brief: Neon tube sputters and dies with a crackle; knobs: tube size (small|medium|large), crackle 0..1, stutter count 0..1, zap brightness 0..1, decay tail toggle

flaws: The sputter bursts are flat, rectangular blocks of broadband noise. They read as gated white-noise static, not a neon tube. There is no clear harmonic buzz stack (mains hum and its overtones) driving each flicker, only a thin low band under the hiss.
Burst edges are hard on/off gates with no ignition ping or arc transient, so the sputters sound mechanical rather than electrical.

At every range minimum the stutters merge into one dull, low blob (centroid 351 Hz, almost no high end) that then decays. The 'flicker' identity is lost; it reads as a muffled thump/hum rather than a tube failing.
Tube size mostly shifts brightness and level. It does not audibly change the hum pitch or the buzz character the way a different-sized tube would, so the choice feels like an EQ preset.
Every render is normalised to peak 0.9, so the 'dies' arc has no loudness story. The flicker bursts never get weaker or more strained as the tube fails; only the post-burst tail decays.
grades.lesson: When a sound is defined by an electrical or mechanical source, build its core from that source's actual spectral signature (e.g. a harmonic buzz comb at mains frequency and its overtones), and add noise only as texture on top. Gated broadband noise reads as generic static at every setting.

flaws: The opening is a flat, full-level wall of buzz about 0.35 s long. It has no flicker or amplitude instability inside it, so it reads as a gated noise block rather than an unstable tube arcing.
The stutter bursts are mostly broadband noise slabs, not the tube's harmonic hum switching on and off. The hum bands and the stutters look like two separate layers.
There is no clearly visible bright 'zap' transient anywhere. The default centroid of 641 Hz is low for neon fizz and crackle, so the signature element of the brief is buried.
The decay tail is a smooth low tonal ring-out lasting about half a second, closer to a reverberant hum or sine decay than a dying tube. The crackle in the tail is only a few faint, sparse ticks.
At every-range-minimum the centroid falls to 287 Hz with only two bursts. The result is a dull, muffled thump that barely reads as electrical.
Seeds keep the same overall shape with shifted burst timing, which is acceptable. The default and Seed 2 are close enough that the variety feels thin across takes.
grades.lesson: Make the defining event in the brief (here the zap or crackle) the most visible feature in the spectrogram at defaults and at every extreme, and derive every stage, including the tail, from the same source rather than appending a generic decaying tone.

flaws: Bursts are hard-gated rectangles. Every onset and offset shows as a full-height vertical line in the spectrogram, so each stutter edge clicks digitally instead of sounding like an arc catching.

The neon body reads as broadband low-heavy noise, not a hum. There is no clear harmonic comb at mains frequency (100/120 Hz and multiples), except faintly in the small size, so it sounds more like gated static than a tube.
The decay tail is sparse ticks running to the file edge, and in defaults and seed 3 a final tick sits at the right border. The render ends abruptly instead of the tube dying out.
tail=false ends on a full-level burst with a sustained horizontal line at the end, so the 'dies' part of the brief is lost.
Silence at 30-43% across renders is mostly dead air between widely spaced ticks. The sputter thins out into near-empty seconds rather than a convincing final crackle.
grades.lesson: Never switch a sound on or off with an instant gate: put a few-millisecond fade on every burst edge, and make sure the last event fully decays before the render ends, so stutters don't click and files don't end abruptly.

brief: Loopable 4 s wet tire hiss from passing traffic; knobs: road width (alley|street|avenue), traffic density 0..1, tire spray 0..1, low rumble 0..1, pass rate, loop crossfade toggle

flaws: Road width barely changes anything: alley, street and avenue show the same three-swell pattern with near-identical envelopes. Only the centroid shifts (1314 / 1071 / 1001 Hz). There is no audible change in reverb, density or pass character that would justify a choice knob.
The loop toggle has no visible effect: loop=false looks essentially the same as the default, so it is impossible to tell whether the crossfade does anything.
The low rumble shows as a thin, constant band in the lowest bin that does not swell with each pass. It reads as a static hum rather than tire and road rumble tied to the cars.

Pass swells are broadband noise with no frequency movement. There is no high-frequency spray emphasis or Doppler-like tilt on approach and departure, and a centroid around 1 kHz is dull for wet tire hiss, which should sit brighter.
At the range minimum the render is one pass followed by more than 3 s of thin, near-empty bed. That is thin as a loop, though not broken.
grades.lesson: Every choice option and toggle must produce a clearly visible difference in envelope, density or spectrum. Before shipping, render each option side by side and remove or redesign any knob whose renders look interchangeable.

flaws: Road width choices are nearly indistinguishable. Alley, street and avenue show the same three broadband pass swells with similar envelopes, and centroids differ only by about 1000-1300 Hz. Nothing reads as a narrow reflective alley versus a wide open avenue (no reverb or slap difference, no change in pass spread or distance).

Each pass is a flat, full-band noise swell from bottom to top. There is no brightening on approach or darkening as it leaves, and no hint of a doppler-like spectral sweep, so it reads as gated noise rather than tyres throwing water.

Wet spray character is weak. The default centroid of about 1 kHz and broadband texture lack the dominant sizzle above 3-4 kHz that sells wet tarmac hiss, and the low rumble band is the hottest element at defaults.
The loop toggle shows no visible effect. The loop=false render looks essentially the same as the default, so the crossfade either does nothing audible or is inaudible at the seams.
At maximum, density, pass rate and rumble pile up into an undifferentiated roar (centroid 735 Hz). Individual passes disappear and it reads as a generic noise bed rather than heavy wet traffic.
At minimum, the program produces one isolated pass in the first second and then roughly 3 s of thin bed. This is usable as sparse traffic, but it is lopsided for a 4 s loop.
Density and pass rate appear to overlap in effect. Both mainly change how many swells occur, so the designer has two knobs doing one job.
grades.lesson: Every choice option must produce a render that is clearly different in envelope or spectrum, not just a few hundred Hz of centroid. If you can't name the visual difference between two options, change the underlying acoustics (space, distance, reflections) until you can.

flaws: Road width barely changes anything. Alley, street and avenue show the same three pass swells of similar width and spacing, with only a centroid shift (1314 vs 1001 Hz). An alley should sound close and reflective, with short sharp passes. An avenue should be wide, with longer overlapping passes and more low end. As built, this choice does not deliver what its labels promise.

The loop toggle has no visible effect. The loop=false render is nearly indistinguishable from the default in envelope, level and spectrum. The default's start and end levels do not obviously match either, so the loopability claimed in the brief cannot be confirmed from the renders.

The spectral balance is somewhat dull for wet tire spray. The centroid sits around 1 kHz, and the upper band is no denser than the mids. Wet hiss usually carries its character in a bright 2-8 kHz spray layer.
Peak is identical (0.664) in every render, so output appears hard-normalised. Traffic density and the other intensity knobs therefore change texture but not perceived level in a controllable way.
At every range maximum the result is a uniform broadband wash with no discernible passes. It is usable as a heavy-traffic bed, but the pass identity is lost.
grades.lesson: Every option of a choice knob must change the sound's defining structure (event duration, spacing, envelope, reflections), not just nudge the tone; render each option side by side and confirm a listener could name which is which, and render any toggle on and off to prove it audibly does something.

brief: Neon sign hum with occasional flicker; knobs: tube size (small|medium|large), buzz intensity 0..1, flicker amount 0..1, rain spatter on glass 0..1, hum pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The rain spatter on glass layer, which the title is built around, cannot be found in any render. A rain spatter should show as scattered, irregular broadband ticks. Instead the upper spectrum is a uniform, static hash that looks the same at minimum and maximum. Even the all-maximum render shows no droplet transients outside the flicker cluster.

The default render has no tail. The hum runs at full level to the last sample and stops dead. Nothing indicates it is a seamless loop, so dropped into a scene it ends abruptly, which an ambience must not do. The tail toggle fixes this but defaults to off.

The flicker dropouts are hard gates. They are near-silent notches with clean vertical edges and broadband vertical lines in the spectrogram, which reads as editing clicks, not a gas tube sputtering and re-striking. Seed 3 shows this most clearly.

Every render peaks at exactly 0.85, so the output is being normalized. Flicker and rain amount then change perceived density but not level. Heavy rain plus heavy buzz should be louder than a quiet tube, but it is not.

The hum itself is good. There are clear harmonic bands at the bottom, size moves the centroid sensibly (small 905 Hz, medium 697 Hz, large 470 Hz), and the two seeds place flicker at different times within the same overall shape.
grades.lesson: When a knob names a distinct layer (like rain over a hum), render that knob alone at its maximum and confirm its own signature is plainly visible over everything else. If you cannot point to it in the spectrogram, the layer is too quiet, masked, or not wired up.

flaws: Every render is locked at 2.50 s and there is no duration control. That is far too short for a hum or ambience bed a designer would lay under a scene, and with the tail on, the 0.5 s fade-out makes the default unusable as a loop.

tail = false ends at full level, so its only purpose is looping, but nothing guarantees the cut points join seamlessly. Its start and end amplitudes and flicker state are unrelated, so a click or jump at the loop point is likely.
Rain spatter at defaults shows only a sparse scatter of vertical streaks. It reads more as occasional crackle than rain on glass, so the 'In Rain' half of the title barely registers at defaults.
Tube size changes little. Small, medium and large differ mainly in centroid (712 / 546 / 459 Hz) with near-identical envelopes, so the choice is subtle rather than three clearly different signs.
At the all-minimum extreme the waveform runs as a flat, uniformly dense block. It still reads as hum, but it is a static drone with no character. It is acceptable but bland.
grades.lesson: Any continuous or ambient sound (hums, beds, weather, room tone) must expose a duration knob with a default of at least 10 s, and its no-tail mode must be built to loop seamlessly by matching start and end state. A fixed short render with a fade is not a usable bed.

flaws: The title promises rain, but at defaults the rain spatter barely registers. The spectrogram shows only faint, sparse vertical ticks over the hum, so the default render reads as a plain neon hum rather than 'Neon In Rain'.

Flicker at defaults is a single shallow dip around 1.2 s. Real neon flicker cuts out hard, close to silence, with a restrike buzz. Here it reads more like a gentle amplitude wobble than a failing tube.
The hum level swells and sags slowly across the default and seed renders (lower start, lumpy body). A neon ballast hum should sit at a steady level between flicker events.

Length is fixed at 2.5 s with no duration control. That is short for a hum bed. With tail off the render ends at full level, which is only useful if it loops seamlessly, and nothing here shows that it does.

Range is acceptable. The minimum is a clean low hum (180 Hz centroid) and the maximum is a heavily stuttering, brighter sign (1392 Hz centroid, peak 0.847, no clipping). Small and large tube sizes differ clearly in centroid (712 vs 459 Hz).
The seeds are good: same envelope, with flicker gaps and rain detail in different places.
grades.lesson: Every element named in the title or brief must be clearly audible and visible at default settings. Defaults are the product demo, so a secondary layer such as rain or crowd should not be buried until the user pushes its knob.

brief: Loopable 3 s view from under a shop awning, rain drumming overhead; knobs: awning material (canvas|vinyl|metal), drum intensity 0..1, runoff stream 0..1, muffled street 0..1, loop crossfade toggle

flaws: Every-range-minimum render is still a dense, unbroken wash at lower level (rms 0.086 vs 0.136). Drum intensity at 0 should thin into sparse, individually audible drops on the awning. Instead it only turns down the same texture.

Every-range-maximum is nearly indistinguishable from defaults (centroid 1078 vs 1083 Hz, similar picture). Maxed runoff stream and muffled street add no visible low-frequency rumble or steady trickle band, so those knobs appear to do almost nothing.

At defaults the canvas render reads as generic broadband noise with a low-band smear. It lacks clear, distinct drop transients drumming on a taut surface, which is what makes an awning read as an awning rather than generic rain.
Vinyl and metal have almost the same centroid (1768 vs 1736 Hz). Only metal's faint horizontal resonance lines separate them, and metal's ringing is weak for rain on sheet metal.
Peak is pinned at 0.664 in every render, which suggests hard normalisation. This hides real level differences between intensity settings.
loop=false looks the same as the looped default and ends at full level with no tail or fade. The toggle's effect cannot be seen, and the non-looped version ends abruptly.
grades.lesson: Make each continuous knob change the structure of the sound across its range, such as event density, added layers or spectral bands, not just its gain. Then render each knob's extremes on their own to confirm the change is clearly visible, rather than only checking that something renders.

flaws: At defaults it reads as a dense, even broadband wash. A few low vertical streaks are the only sign of drop impacts. 'Rain drumming overhead' on an awning should show clear individual drop transients and a low thud body above the hiss floor. The spectrogram is near-uniform hiss up to the top band.

loop = false is almost identical to the default render (centroid 1042 vs 1083 Hz, rms 0.139 vs 0.136). It ends at full level with no tail or fade. The toggle does nothing visible, and the non-loop version ends abruptly, which an ambience must not do.

Vinyl (1768 Hz) and metal (1736 Hz) have almost the same centroid and envelope. Only metal's faint horizontal resonance bands set it apart. Vinyl does not read as a distinct surface: it should have a slappier, more plastic patter.

Runoff stream and muffled street leave no clear mark in the min/max renders. Max only shows a lower centroid and slightly higher level. No steady trickle band and no low rumble layer are identifiable, so the bundled ranges look like one tone/level change rather than separate layers.
Peak is exactly 0.664 in every render. This suggests blanket peak normalisation, which hides real level differences between intensity settings.
grades.lesson: Every toggle and knob must produce a visible, purpose-specific change in the render: a loop toggle must change the ending (a seamless wrap vs a natural fade-out), and each layer knob should add its own identifiable band or texture rather than just shifting overall brightness or level.

flaws: Loop seam looks broken with loop on. At defaults and on both seeds the waveform starts noticeably thinner and ends at full density. Wrapping the file would produce an audible level jump, which defeats the 'loopable' brief.
The drumming arrives in clumps with faint, near-regular vertical gaps in the low band, in every render. This reads as a pulsing pattern rather than random rain hitting a surface.
With every range at its minimum, the result is about six isolated drips over a flat line (8% silence). The ambience bed disappears entirely, so this setting is not usable as a continuous loop.

The metal setting shows steady horizontal tonal bands throughout. That is plausible ring, but it is constant and does not respond to individual hits, so it sounds more like a hum than struck sheet metal.
Material choices are clearly distinct (centroid 544/962/1413 Hz). Seeds read as takes of one sound. The maximum is dense without clipping (peak 0.9). The loop=false tail-off is clean.
grades.lesson: For any loopable ambience, compare the first and last ~200 ms of the render for matching level and event density before shipping. Keep a continuous low bed under sparse events so that minimum settings never produce silent gaps.

brief: Single car passing over wet road left-to-right; knobs: vehicle (compact|sedan|truck|bus), speed 0..1, spray amount 0..1, engine presence 0..1, doppler pitch, tail toggle

flaws: No tonal engine component visible in any render. The spectrogram is pure broadband noise with no harmonic lines, so 'engine presence' does not read.
No Doppler pitch drop anywhere: no falling line through the pass point, even with every range at maximum. A defining cue of a pass-by is missing.

The envelope is a symmetric noise swell. A real wet pass rises gradually, then drops sharply after the car passes into a lingering spray or wake hiss. This reads as filtered noise with a fade in and out.
tail = false is nearly identical to the default (rms 0.142 vs 0.138, silence 14% vs 13%, same shape). The toggle has no meaningful effect.

Vehicle types are barely distinct: truck vs compact is only a modest centroid shift (1809 vs 2263 Hz). There is no heavier low-end rumble or tyre and engine character for the truck, and the bus was not shown.
The renders give no evidence of left-to-right panning (the waveform is mono).
grades.lesson: Before submitting, render each knob at its extremes and confirm the change is visible in the spectrogram or the numbers. Pitch effects like Doppler must show as moving lines, tonal sources must show as harmonics, and toggles must alter the envelope. A knob whose effect cannot be seen should be fixed or removed.

flaws: All-minimum render is broken. With slow speed and no spray it peaks early, then holds near full level until the file cuts off at 3.71 s, with no recession or decay. The pass-by never finishes and ends in an abrupt chop.

The all-minimum render also collapses to a 173 Hz rumble at almost twice the default RMS (0.25 vs 0.145). It reads as a low drone, not a car passing on a wet road. Level is not compensated across the range.
Doppler pitch drop is weak at defaults. The engine harmonics bend only slightly at the closest point, so the pass-by lacks the falling-pitch signature a designer expects.
