Vehicle choices differ only modestly. Compact and truck sit at 2328 Hz and 1887 Hz centroid with similar envelopes, and the truck lacks the expected weight and low-end dominance. Sedan and bus were not demonstrated.
The brief asks for left-to-right movement, but nothing in the renders shows panning or stereo motion, so this cannot be verified.
Each render has only about 0.3–0.5 s of lead-in, so the approach swell is short for a wet-road pass.
grades.lesson: Derive render length from the parameters that control event timing, such as speed, distance and size, so that at every extreme the event completes and decays to silence inside the file. Compensate level across the range so that extreme settings don't jump far above or below the default loudness.

flaws: The defining pass-by cue is missing. At defaults the low engine harmonics run as flat horizontal lines across the spectrogram, with no visible pitch fall at the moment of closest approach. The 'doppler pitch' knob either does nothing at its default or is far too subtle. Without the drop, this reads as a crossfade of hiss, not a car going by.

In the all-max render the low engine lines run from the left edge into the peak and then cut off rather than dropping in pitch and fading. The engine appears to vanish after the pass instead of receding.
The tyre spray is a smooth, uniform broadband wash. It lacks the gritty, modulated hiss-and-slosh texture of tyres on wet asphalt. It reads closer to filtered white noise with an amplitude envelope.
The speed range is narrow in practice: the full sweep only moves duration from 3.98 s to 2.90 s. A fast car on a wet road should give a noticeably shorter, sharper pass than a crawl.
Left-to-right panning, a core part of the brief, cannot be verified from these renders. Nothing in the shape suggests the spatial movement drives the spectral change.
grades.lesson: When a sound's identity rests on one physical cue (Doppler drop, pitch sweep, transient), make that cue unmistakable at default settings and check that it shows up visibly in the spectrogram. A matching envelope alone does not make the sound read correctly.

brief: Water rushing into a curbside storm drain; knobs: grate size (small|medium|large), flow 0..1, gurgle 0..1, sewer echo 0..1, gulp rate, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the render is a mostly continuous broadband noise wash with faint low blips. There are no clear, repeated gulp events, which the title and the 'gulp rate' knob promise. It reads as generic rushing water or hiss, not a drain swallowing.

With every range at minimum, a weak low trickle is interrupted at about 2.1 s by one huge broadband spike, followed by sparse vertical clicks and gaps (12% silence). This looks like a click or discontinuity artifact rather than a water event.
Because every render is peak-normalised to 0.9, that lone spike sets the level and buries the actual trickle.
grate=small has the same problem: an isolated, sharp, full-height transient at about 2.6 s dominates the file and reads like a pop, not water.
With every range at maximum there is a sustained horizontal red band in the low-mids. It looks like a steady tonal hum and is likely to sound synthetic rather than like turbulent water.
The gurgle and sewer echo are hard to distinguish across renders. The echo tail is only a short fade, with no audible pipe resonance or reflections.
Large and small grate differ mainly in brightness and level, not in character (for example, the trickle-through-slots of a small grate versus the open gulp of a large one).
grades.lesson: Make sure the event named in the title is clearly visible and audible at defaults, and never let a single isolated transient set the peak normalisation. When the background layers are quiet, cap or smooth stray impulses so they do not become a click that dominates the whole file.

flaws: At defaults the spectrogram is a nearly uniform broadband haze with energy piled in the bottom band. There are no short tonal blips or chirps of the kind bubbles and gurgles produce, so this reads as filtered noise or a whoosh rather than water pouring through a grate.

The gurgle character is not visible in any render. Even with every range at maximum, only a smeared low-mid band appears, not discrete resonant gulps, so the gurgle and gulp-rate knobs seem to modulate noise loudness rather than add liquid events.
The envelope is the same swell-and-decay shape in every render, including grate size, all-min, all-max and both seeds. Range extremes change brightness and length but not behaviour.
The seeds are very close to identical takes (centroid 946/936/948 Hz, RMS 0.261/0.258/0.261). Detail differs, but there is little take-to-take variation in where the gulps fall.
With tail=false the sound still runs 2.66 s and ends in a soft fade, so the toggle mostly trims rather than removing the tail.
Every render peaks at exactly 0.9, which suggests normalisation. That flattens the loudness difference you would expect between low and high flow.
grades.lesson: For liquid sounds, broadband noise alone reads as wind or a whoosh. Add discrete resonant events (short pitched bubble chirps and gurgles that sweep in frequency) and check that they show up as tonal streaks in the spectrogram before submitting.

flaws: Every-range-minimum render falls apart. It is sparse, isolated spiky clicks with gaps (17% silence) that read as ticking or drips on metal, not water draining. A low-flow trickle should still be continuous water.

Defaults are mostly broadband noise surges. The spectrogram shows few of the resonant, pitched bubble or gurgle traces that sell a drain 'gulp', so it reads closer to generic filtered rush or rain-on-pavement than water swallowed by a grate.
The tail region of defaults and large grate is sparse clicky ticks after the main body rather than a draining slurp or echo decay. This makes the ending feel tacked on.
Seed 2 jumps to near full level almost instantly and holds a flat block, which is less natural than the swelling surges of the other takes.
On the positive side, grate size behaves well: small is brighter and shorter, large is darker and longer. Max range is a dense, plausible torrent.
grades.lesson: Render every knob at its minimum and confirm it is still a quieter or smaller version of the same sound. Low ends of density or flow parameters must thin the texture gradually, not collapse it into isolated clicks and gaps.

brief: Distant emergency siren drifting across the skyline; knobs: siren type (police|ambulance|fire), distance 0..1, building reflections 0..1, rain masking 0..1, wail rate, fade tail toggle

flaws: A notch/dropout sits at the same spot (~1.8 s) in the defaults, seed 2 and tail=false renders. It looks like a bad splice or crossfade between two halves of the render, and an editor would hear it as a hiccup in the siren.

At maximum, the siren tone is almost buried under broadband noise. Only a faint line survives low in the spectrum, so the render reads as rain with a hint of something rather than a siren. There is also a stray transient spike around 1.4 s.

Seeds 2 and 3 share an almost identical pitch contour and envelope as the defaults. Only the noise grain differs, so these are not two distinct takes: wail phase, sweep timing and drift should change per seed.
Every render is a fixed 3.5 s regardless of settings. That is short for a siren 'drifting across the skyline', and there is no visible Doppler pitch drift or slow pass-by arc to sell the movement.
At minimum, the siren is a dry, perfectly regular harmonic stack. It reads as a synthetic sawtooth rather than a real siren horn, even when close.
With tail=false the sound runs at full level to the last sample and stops dead, with no short release to avoid a click.
grades.lesson: When a render is assembled from segments, loops or crossfaded halves, inspect the waveform at every join and use equal-power, phase-aware crossfades: a level notch at a splice point is audible and repeats in every render that uses that structure.

flaws: A narrow notch or dropout appears in the middle of the waveform: about 1.9 s at defaults, about 1.6 s on seed 2, and a pronounced dip in the tail=false render. It looks like a segment-join or crossfade glitch, and it will be heard as a click or hole in a sustained siren.

With every range at maximum, the siren is almost completely buried. Only a faint line remains under broadband noise (centroid 2003 Hz, rms 0.135). It reads as rain with a hint of something, not a distant siren behind rain.

With every range at minimum, the render is a sterile, perfectly regular harmonic stack with a swollen, near-constant body. It reads as a test oscillator, not a real siren even up close, and it has no reflections or air.

Defaults are supposed to be distant, but they keep a fairly bright harmonic stack. There is little air absorption or low-pass to sell the distance, and drifting across the skyline shows only as a slow pitch arc, with no sense of movement or Doppler.
Seeds 1-3 have almost identical sweep trajectories and envelopes. Only the noise detail changes, so the wail timing and phase do not vary between takes.
tail=false cuts off hard at 3.5 s. The start and end are not matched for looping, so it is neither a clean loop nor a finished one-shot.
Peak is exactly 0.691 in every render, which suggests hard normalisation. As a result, the distance and rain knobs do not change perceived level the way a designer expects.
grades.lesson: When a sound is built from joined segments or a toggled envelope stage, render it and inspect the joins for notches, dropouts or discontinuities. Crossfade every boundary with equal-power overlap so that no edit point is visible in the waveform.

flaws: A dropout or discontinuity appears mid-render, around 1.6–1.8 s. It shows as a sharp vertical notch in the seed 2 waveform, a smaller one at defaults, and a dip in the tail=false render. It looks like a segment or loop boundary that is not crossfaded, and it would be audible as a click or gap.
At every range at maximum, the siren is buried under the rain and reflection noise. The spectrogram is mostly a broadband wash with only a faint tonal line, so the setting no longer reads as a siren.
At maximum, the render ends at substantial level instead of fading. The ambience is cut off abruptly.
With tail=false, the render ends abruptly at full level, and the mid-file dip means it also cannot serve as a clean loop. The toggle produces neither a usable loop nor a finished one-shot.
Length is fixed at 3.5 s and there is no duration knob. That is too short for a distant siren drifting across a skyline, and the fade-out takes up nearly half the file.
Nothing in the render conveys 'drifting across': there is no Doppler, pan or approach/recede movement, and no knob for it. The brief's central motion is missing.
The ambulance setting shows only weak hi-lo steps and reads as an almost static tone.
grades.lesson: When a sound is built from concatenated segments or alternating states, crossfade every boundary. Before submitting, inspect the waveform at every seed and toggle for vertical notches or dropouts. Also make sure no parameter extreme lets a masking layer bury the sound's defining element.

flaws: No clear Doppler pitch drop. The brief names doppler pitch as a knob, but no falling harmonic line crosses the pass peak in any render. The low band stays a flat smear, so the pass-by reads more as a noise swell than a vehicle going past.
The engine's tonal component is weak. Broadband spray hiss dominates every render, and there are only faint low harmonics at the bottom of the spectrogram, even for truck.
The envelope is a near-symmetric diamond. Real pass-bys usually have a sharper rise into the closest point and a longer receding tail, so this looks synthetic.
Vehicle types differ mainly in centroid and level (compact brighter, truck lower and louder). There is no strong change in timbre or engine character between them.
Left-to-right panning cannot be checked from the mono renders.
regrade.lesson: When a brief names a pitch-motion effect such as Doppler, make it unmistakable in the spectrogram at defaults. A tonal component should visibly bend downward through the event's peak; it should not be buried under broadband noise.

flaws: A 'drifting across the skyline' pass is compressed into 3.5 s with a fixed fade. Default police shows barely one slow wail cycle before dying, so it plays as a short one-shot rather than a usable distant siren bed or pass-by. There is no duration or pass-length control.

The only sense of drift is the amplitude fade-out. There is no visible approach or swell, and no pitch bend from motion (Doppler) as the source crosses. It reads as 'siren turning off', not 'siren moving across the city'.
At max ranges, rain masking and reflections bury the siren. The tonal line is barely visible under a broadband noise wash, so the extreme reads as rain with a faint hum rather than a siren in rain.
The max render does not fade out. The level holds to the last frame, so that extreme ends abruptly even though the defaults fade.
The default, ambulance and seed renders share a mid-file amplitude notch at the same point, most visible in seed 2. It looks like a structural dropout rather than natural occlusion.
Seeds 2 and 3 are near-identical to the default in wail timing and contour. Variation is limited to noise detail, so two takes would not sound like separate sirens on separate nights.
regrade.lesson: When a brief describes motion or a long-lived event (drifting, passing, approaching), give the render enough duration to show that motion and model it explicitly with a level swell, a pitch shift and a spectral change. Also cap masking/mix knobs so the subject stays dominant at their extremes.

flaws: At defaults the low band shows drum bursts at near-regular intervals (about 0.3 s). The drumming reads slightly mechanical rather than the random patter of rain hitting fabric.

With every range at its minimum, the sound collapses to about 8 evenly spaced isolated drops over near-dead air. This reads as slow drips, not rain on an awning, and the even spacing exposes a metronomic scheduler.
There is no floor bed (light hiss or room tone) at minimum intensity, so a 3 s loop at low settings would have audible holes in a scene.
The defaults are quite dark (centroid 544 Hz). Canvas drumming lacks the bright splash layer at the top that gives rain its texture; only metal and vinyl get much high-frequency detail.
regrade.lesson: For any rain or particle ambience, draw impact times from a random (Poisson-style) process with jitter, never a near-fixed interval. Always keep a quiet continuous bed under the impacts even at the lowest intensity, so the sparsest setting reads as light rain rather than isolated metronomic drips over silence.

flaws: The 'echoing down a block' never reads as street echo. At defaults the horn is a ~0.45 s harmonic burst followed by a smooth exponential decay. The spectrogram shows no discrete slapback reflections, no rhythmic repeats and no late-reflection pattern, so it looks like a reverb tail rather than a honk bouncing off building faces.
Nothing in any render suggests 'wet'. There is no broadband road-hiss or tyre-spray layer and no damped high-frequency reflection character, so the second half of the brief is absent.

The horn timbre is thin for a car horn. Harmonics are visible, but energy is concentrated in the bottom few partials and the centroid sits at ~890 Hz. A real horn's brassy upper partials, which make it cut through a mix, are weak.

The compact choice behaves unlike the others. It produces three chopped, tremolo-like bursts that read more like a stuttering gate or a deliberate beep-beep-beep than one honk with echo. It also smears a broad mid-high noise wash across the spectrogram and leaves isolated vertical ticks near the end of the file, which look like clicks or artifacts.
Choice extremes are distinct (truck is properly low at 523 Hz, compact is bright), but compact's different envelope means the horn-type knob changes the event structure, not just the vehicle.

The two seeds differ mainly in burst length and tail level. Both reasonable, but neither shows variation in reflection timing, which is where natural take-to-take difference in a street echo would live.
The tail toggle overlaps conceptually with street echo and length. Its role relative to the echo amount is unclear from the renders.
regrade.lesson: When a brief names a spatial behaviour (echo down a street, slap off a wall, reflections in a canyon), build it as discrete, audible delayed copies with spacing and filtering derived from the geometry, not as a generic decay or reverb tail. The listener identifies the space from distinct reflections, and a smooth fade reads as 'reverb' rather than 'place'.

flaws: At defaults the hum fades out over the last ~0.4 s. A neon hum bed is mostly used as a loop, so a default fade-out makes it awkward to drop in until the tail toggle is turned off.
Flicker dips in the waveform look rounded and swell-like rather than the abrupt on/off dropouts of a failing neon ballast. The spectrogram gaps are there, but their edges are soft.
Rain spatter is barely visible at defaults: only faint broadband vertical streaks high in the spectrogram. The 'In Rain' part of the title is underplayed.
Small and large tube sizes differ mainly in centroid (712 vs 459 Hz) and look structurally similar. The choice could change harmonic density or buzz character more distinctly.
At the all-max extreme the dips become deep and frequent enough that it starts to read as a sputtering engine rather than a sign. It is usable, but it sits at the edge of the sound's identity.
regrade.lesson: For continuous sources such as hums, drones and ambiences, make the default render loop-friendly with steady level at both ends, and put any fade-out tail behind an opt-in toggle rather than leaving it on by default.

brief: Umbrella snapping open with water shake; knobs: umbrella type (compact|golf|clear dome), snap force 0..1, fabric rustle 0..1, droplet shake 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The droplet tail is a train of isolated, nearly evenly spaced ticks that thin out over a second. It reads more like a ratchet or clock winding down than water flung off fabric. A real shake gives a dense spray burst tied to the shake motion, then a few irregular stragglers.

The three umbrella types look almost the same: same envelope and same tail pattern, with only a modest centroid shift (1597–2116 Hz). Golf should be noticeably bigger and lower, and clear dome stiffer and crinklier (plastic), with a different snap and rustle character.
The snap itself is a broadband smear with low-end weight but no distinct latch click separate from the fabric whoosh. The 'pop-open then lock' structure of a real umbrella is underdefined.
About 40% silence across a 1.6 s file with sparse ticks leaves the tail sounding empty rather than wet.
grades.lesson: When scattering secondary particles (droplets, debris, sparks), randomise their spacing and cluster them around the motion that causes them, with density following the cause. Evenly spaced, decaying single ticks read as a mechanical ratchet, not a natural spray.

flaws: Burst on/off edges are rectangular. The spectrogram shows hard vertical walls, so each sputter starts and stops like a gate rather than a gas discharge striking and quenching, which reads slightly synthetic.

The sputter bursts are dominated by broadband noise wash over the hum harmonics. The characteristic tonal neon buzz (strong mains-harmonic comb) is present but buried, especially at large size and at minimum ranges.

Small crackle ticks run right up to the last pixel in several renders (defaults, seed 2, size small, size large, max). The final event may be truncated by the file end instead of decaying out, so the 'dies' moment is not clearly resolved.
The 'zap' is only visible as one short burst with a falling partial near the end. Zap brightness has little distinct visual identity separate from the overall brightness.
regrade.lesson: For any sound that ends in sparse events (ticks, debris, drips), schedule the last event early enough that its full decay plus a short silent margin fits before the file ends, so the sound resolves instead of being cut mid-event.

flaws: The attack fades in over roughly 0.1 s instead of starting with a sharp impact. A tire hitting deep water should open with a sudden hit, but this one swells in like a whoosh.
There is no low-frequency 'whomp' from the water being displaced. The spectrogram's bottom band is faint and quickly gone, so the body has no weight.

The body of the sound is uniform broadband noise with no visible liquid structure. It shows no sheet-tearing streaks, no bubbly modulation and no rising or falling motion of the sheet, so it reads as a shaped noise burst rather than water.
Curb slap at maximum shows no distinct slap transient in the 'every range at its maximum' render. That knob's character is not legible.

The 'every range at its maximum' and 'every range at its minimum' renders share almost the same envelope; the main differences are length and brightness. Speed does not visibly sharpen the onset or increase how violent the sound is.
The droplet tail is reasonable but sparse and regular. It carries most of the realism that the main splash lacks.
regrade.lesson: For impact-driven sounds such as splashes, crashes and hits, build the event from layers that are each visible in the spectrogram: a sharp broadband front edge, a low-frequency body, and a textured mid layer with the material's own modulation. A single noise burst with a smooth envelope reads as generic hiss, not as the material.

brief: Umbrella collapsed and shaken out under shelter; knobs: umbrella type (compact|golf|clear dome), shake count 0..1, spray 0..1, strap click 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The shake impacts carry steady low horizontal bands (roughly 80-150 Hz) that read as pitched synthetic thumps rather than broadband canopy flaps. They are especially prominent in the tail=false render.
With tail=false the render ends on a noise burst and transient right at the last sample, which looks like a hard cut. It should decay or fade, even if that final event is the strap click.
The strap click is not clearly distinguishable in the default or extreme renders. It is hard to tell where it sits or whether it reads as a click versus more fabric noise.
Clear dome thins out the shakes and pushes the centroid to about 3.4 kHz, but its low thumps still look similar to the other types. The type changes the hiss more than it changes the body.
Seeds 2 and 3 are very close to the default in shake timing. Most of the variation is in the drip tail rather than in the shake rhythm or the intensity of individual shakes.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes the tail or shortens a sound, make sure the last event still gets its full natural decay plus a short fade, so the shortened variant never ends on a truncated transient.

flaws: Individual passes show up as static vertical bands of broadband noise with no spectral motion. There is no visible approach/recede filter sweep or Doppler tilt, so each pass reads as a gated noise swell rather than a tire hissing past.
The low rumble is a thin constant line at the very bottom of the spectrogram. It does not swell with the passes, so it sounds like a separate drone rather than vehicle body noise.

The road-width choices are only subtly different. Alley vs avenue mostly shifts the centroid by ~300 Hz with no clear change in reflection or density character, so a designer may not hear a reason to switch.
Traffic density and pass rate appear to overlap in effect. At max both just produce an undifferentiated wash.
regrade.lesson: For pass-by or moving-source sounds, give each event spectral motion (a lowpass or tilt sweep that opens on approach and closes on recede, plus slight pitch drift), and tie any low-end layer to the same event envelope so the parts read as one object rather than gated noise over a drone.

flaws: At defaults the body reads as broadband noise with some low gurgle bursts, but there is little sense of a steady rushing bed feeding the drain. It plays as a single swell-and-fade event, not water continuously pouring into a grate.

The all-minimum render collapses into isolated clicky impulses with near-silent gaps (17% silence). It reads as crackle or drips rather than a thin trickle of water, so the low end of the flow range breaks the identity of the sound.
The max render is a dense, featureless wash with the gurgle detail smeared out. The upper extreme loses the gulping character the title promises.
The tail's sparse high ticks look more like isolated clicks than a sewer reverb. The sewer echo control does not visibly produce a diffuse, low, resonant decay.
Grate size works well, shifting the centroid and length across 1836/967/642 Hz in a sensible direction. The two seeds read as two takes of one sound. The flaws above are the problem.
regrade.lesson: For a continuous fluid source, keep a continuous noise bed underneath the discrete events at every knob setting. Low settings should thin and darken the bed, never gate it into isolated impulses with silence between them.

brief: City bus pulls in with wet brakes and air hiss; knobs: bus size (mini|standard|articulated), brake squeal 0..1, air release 0..1, splash 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the brake squeal is only a faint, broken tonal line around the mid band. The 'wet brakes' character the brief leads with barely registers until the squeal knob is pushed up.

The air release bursts are very short vertical bands (roughly 0.1-0.2 s). A real bus kneeling or door 'psssht' is a longer hiss with a decaying tail, so the event reads more like a burst of noise than an air release.
The low engine bed is a series of ticks with no visible downward pitch or rate glide. The bus does not clearly decelerate as it pulls in.
With every range at its minimum, the air release and squeal almost vanish, leaving mainly a rumble-and-splash wash. That extreme no longer reads strongly as a bus arrival.
grades.lesson: Make every signature event named in the brief clearly audible at the default settings and give it a realistic duration. A feature that only appears at the knob extreme, or a hiss that lasts a tenth of a second, makes the default render read as a generic wash rather than the specific thing described.

brief: Rain pattering on an umbrella from the holder's ear; knobs: canopy (nylon|vinyl|paper), rain density 0..1, drop size 0..1, drip-off edge 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the bed runs at full level to the last sample and cuts off. There is no fade-out and no evidence of a loop-safe seam, so the sound ends abruptly.
With tail on, the rain stops fairly suddenly around 2.6 s before the drip-off. The drop-out reads more like a cut than the rain easing off.
At the range minimum the render shortens to 2.0 s, so duration appears coupled to density or drop size. A designer would not expect a density knob to change the length of an ambience.
grades.lesson: For any ambience or bed, either make the render seamlessly loopable or give it a short fade-out at the end. Keep total duration independent of character knobs like density, so turning one knob never changes the clip length unexpectedly.

brief: Car door opening and shutting in rain; knobs: vehicle (compact|sedan|taxi|van), slam force 0..1, seal squelch 0..1, rain inside 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Vehicle choices differ mainly in when the slam lands (compact 1.82 s, taxi 2.23 s). The slam itself has nearly the same spectrum in each (centroid 1376-1482 Hz, same low-end blob), so a compact does not read as lighter or a van as heavier.
The rain bed sits far below the slam (default RMS 0.057 against peak 0.79), and 14-16% of frames measure as silent. That is a thin rain layer rather than a dense, gapless wet ambience.

The rain does not visibly get louder or brighter while the door is open. The opening latch clicks and the slam sit over an unchanging bed, so the 'rain inside' knob is not reflected in an open-door section of the timeline.
The rain noise runs right to the end of the file, most clearly with tail=false at 1.52 s. The ending risks sounding like a hard cut of the rain bed instead of a fade.
With every range at minimum, the slam is weak and nearly lost in the rain. It is still usable but borders on a non-event.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names physically different objects (small vs large, light vs heavy), make each option change the spectrum and decay of the main event, such as resonant pitch, low-end weight and ring length, not just its timing. Otherwise every option renders as the same sound shifted in time.

brief: Single footstep into a shallow puddle; knobs: shoe (sneaker|boot|heel|leather), splash depth 0..1, weight 0..1, grit 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Sneaker and heel are effectively the same sound. Centroid is 2708 vs 2711 Hz, with near-identical envelopes and spectrograms. A heel on wet ground should have a hard, narrow, bright click at the attack, and a sneaker a soft rubbery slap. Here both are the same broadband splash, so the headline shoe choice does not deliver.

The impact and splash are one undifferentiated ~0.3 s broadband noise wash. There is no distinct sole contact followed by the water displacement, so the step reads more as 'something splashed' than a foot landing in a puddle.
Roughly 40-50% of every render is trailing near-silence after the last droplet. Editors will have to trim the dead tail on every placement.

The all-minimum and all-maximum renders differ only modestly in brightness and level. The splash depth and weight extremes do not produce the shallow-tap versus heavy-stomp contrast the knob names promise.
The droplet tail is sparse and a little random-blippy, with isolated ticks scattered out to ~0.45 s. It lacks a convincing short spatter cluster right after the impact.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names materials or objects, make each option change the attack transient itself (duration, brightness, resonance), not just a shared noise layer. Then verify the options measure clearly apart, for example in centroid and attack length, before shipping.

flaws: At defaults the first ~150 ms is a train of evenly spaced amplitude bumps, roughly every 8 ms (about 120 Hz AM), with a hot low band underneath. That reads as a buzzy, resonant thud, not a noisy splash. Real water spray is irregular and broadband, not periodic.
The tail=false render exposes it clearly: a regular pulse train with a sustained low-frequency band. It sounds more like a flutter or motorboat than a foot entering water.

The bottom-octave energy lasts ~0.3 s in the default, sneaker and max renders. A shallow puddle step should have a short low thump, then mid/high spray and droplet blips. The lingering low rumble muddies it.
The droplet blips after the splash are present but sparse and faint. The bubbly, tonal 'plip' character that sells water is underplayed compared with the resonant body.

Heel and sneaker read convincingly as distinct shoes, with a sharp transient and a heel-toe second hit. The water layer itself barely changes across choices, so the shoe knob carries most of the range.
The min and max extremes stay in family, and the two seeds look like good takes of one sound. Neither fixes the core periodic-modulation problem.
grades.lesson: When building splashes, crunches or other noisy impacts, make sure no oscillator, LFO or comb/resonator puts evenly spaced amplitude bumps in the waveform. Natural noisy events have irregular micro-structure, so randomise grain timing and keep low-frequency resonances short (under ~80 ms) unless the brief calls for a ringing body.

flaws: The body of the splash is mostly broadband filtered noise. There are almost no visible tonal bubble or droplet blips in the tail (only a few faint marks around the middle of the spectrogram), so it may read as a gritty scuff on wet gravel rather than water.
The sneaker render is nearly indistinguishable from defaults (0.54 vs 0.51 s, centroid 2653 vs 2485 Hz). The shoe choice does not separate sole types much, apart from heel.
The heel render shows no distinct hard click at the attack. It is just a brighter, shorter wash, so it lacks the sharp heel-tap transient a designer would expect.
The impact thump at the bottom of the spectrum is weak at defaults. The low-end energy is a thin band with no clear weighted foot-plant body.
The all-maximum render runs 0.71 s with a long dense noise wash. It edges toward a splash ambience rather than a single step.
grades.lesson: When a sound's identity comes from a material (water, glass, metal), model that material's signature: short pitched bubble or droplet resonances for water, ringing modes for glass or metal. Shaped noise alone reads as generic grit.

brief: Footstep on rain-slick sidewalk; knobs: shoe (sneaker|boot|heel|leather), weight 0..1, squelch 0..1, scuff 0..1, step rate, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the waveform after the heel strike is a regular, evenly spaced oscillation lasting about 0.3 s. It reads as a struck resonant body, like a low tom or a plucked box, not a shoe meeting wet concrete. A wet step should be a broadband slap followed by irregular, noisy splash and squelch detail.

The spectrum is too dark for rain-slick pavement. The centroid is about 470-600 Hz for every shoe except heel, and most of the energy sits on a low band at the bottom of the spectrogram. Little bright splash or spray noise appears in the 2-8 kHz region, where 'wet' would be heard.

The maximum-range render makes the ringing worse. It shows about 15 clean decaying cycles, close to a drum hit, so the weight and squelch extremes push the sound further toward the wrong kind of sound instead of a heavier, wetter step.

Seed 3 is strongly periodic and ringing while the default seed is noisier. The two takes differ in character, not just in detail, so the ringing appears to be an unstable artifact rather than a designed component.
With the tail on, a single step lasts about 0.73 s with roughly 40% silence. The decay drags on longer than a dry step needs, and the extra length is resonant ringing, not wet ambience or drip.
With tail = false the waveform shows several lumpy secondary bursts. These read more like a wobble than a clean scuff or squelch.
The 'step rate' knob does little for a one-shot step render. A designer would rather have a wetness or splash-amount control, or a puddle-depth control, that adds bright spray noise.
grades.lesson: When you model an impact on a surface, check the waveform tail for evenly spaced oscillation. A long, regular ringing decay means a resonator or filter is dominating, and the sound will read as a struck instrument instead of the material contact you were asked for. Damp the resonance heavily and let shaped broadband noise carry the tail.

flaws: The impact lacks a body. Every render is mostly broadband noise with a 3.0–3.6 kHz centroid. There is only a faint low-frequency spot at the onset, so it reads more as a wet splash or spray burst than a foot landing on concrete.

The shoe choices barely differ. Sneaker, heel and default look nearly the same: same peak, a similar noise wash, and centroids within about 200 Hz. A heel should be a hard, short, ringing click and a sneaker a soft, dull thud, but sneaker actually comes out brighter than default.

The 'drips' after the step are isolated narrow ticks scattered at random late in the render. They look like stray clicks or artifacts rather than water settling, and they make the tail feel unfinished.
At the maximum range the splash and squelch wash runs about 0.4 s at high RMS. It starts to sound like a puddle stomp or wave, not a step on a slick sidewalk.
A step-rate knob does not belong in a single-shot footstep asset. It either does nothing useful in a one-shot render or belongs in the game's trigger logic.
grades.lesson: Every value of a categorical choice (material, shoe, surface) must change the core envelope and spectrum in a way you can see. Different attack sharpness, body frequency and decay length should make each option recognisable on its own. Shared noise layers should not dominate, and render-to-render differences should not shrink to small centroid shifts.

flaws: The default sneaker step has no clean impact transient. The waveform is a train of six or seven similar-sized low-frequency bumps across the first 0.2 s, which reads as a muddy wobble or gurgle rather than a foot striking hard pavement.

The wet surface is missing from the spectrum. The default centroid is 365 Hz with energy piled into the bottom band. A rain-slick sidewalk should show a firm mid-frequency contact and a short burst of bright high-frequency water spatter, and neither is visible. It reads more like stepping in mud than on wet concrete.

The heel choice is the only variant with a convincing hard-surface transient (2490 Hz, with crisp separate heel and toe clicks). It looks dry, though, with no splash content, so it does not read as the same wet-sidewalk sound as the other shoes. It feels like a different patch.
The maximum-range render keeps a low red band for most of its 0.43 s under a broad noisy mid wash. That is close to the 'wash instead of a step' failure, and the transient definition is lost.
A 'step rate' knob makes little sense on a one-shot footstep asset, since timing belongs to the game engine or editor. Its slot would be better spent on wetness or surface depth (puddle versus damp).
grades.lesson: For impact sounds, build the strike first as one sharp, broadband onset whose loudest peak lands in the first few milliseconds. Put surface character (water, grit, squelch) on top as a separate, brighter layer that decays quickly. Do not let a resonant low-frequency body make many equal peaks that blur the attack into a muddy wobble.

brief: Wet raincoat movement and zipper; knobs: fabric (vinyl|nylon|wool), movement 0..1, water squeak 0..1, zipper presence 0..1, speed, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 1.2s but the default render is 2.24s

flaws: The rustle is smooth enveloped broadband noise. The spectrogram shows even blue slabs instead of the dense crinkly transients that vinyl or nylon movement produces, so it reads more like shaped hiss than fabric.

The zipper is not identifiable at defaults or at any extreme. There is no run of rapid, regularly spaced teeth ticks. The only discrete events are a few sparse clicks in the tail, which read as drips, not a zip.
The water squeak is barely present: a single faint horizontal line in the first burst. At defaults it adds almost nothing a designer would hear as wet rubbery squeak.

Every render, including the seeds and both range extremes, has the same two-burst-then-sparse-ticks structure. The movement and speed ranges change density only slightly, so the extremes barely differ in gesture.
With tail = false the render ends on a full-level burst at the file edge, which is close to an abrupt cut.
Wool sits oddly in a raincoat brief. It does read clearly darker (1114 Hz centroid) with low thumps, so it is the one choice that is well differentiated.
grades.lesson: When a brief names several distinct components (e.g. rustle plus zipper plus squeak), give each its own characteristic time-frequency signature at default settings: zipper as a fast regular tick train, squeak as a gliding tonal line, fabric as dense irregular transients. Check that each is visibly identifiable in the spectrogram rather than merged into one band of filtered noise.

flaws: tail = false is broken: the render does not fade or end on silence. It stops on a sustained, full-level buzzy block at 1.35 s, which will click and sound like a cut file. Its layout also changes to three bursts with a constant-level middle section, so the toggle changes the event structure instead of only removing the drips.

The water squeak draws as long, steady horizontal sine lines lasting about 0.3–0.5 s, some gently falling. Real wet-fabric squeaks are short, irregular chirps, so this reads synthetic, like a whistle under the rustle.
The zipper does not show up as a ratcheting row of evenly spaced tooth clicks at defaults. Only wool's opening comb-like section looks zipper-ish, so 'zipper presence' is hard to read across fabrics.
The post-movement drip tail is very sparse: a few isolated ticks over about 0.8 s, leaving 26–45% of the file near-silent. That is acceptable but thin.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes a section such as a tail, end the sound with a proper release envelope to silence. Never truncate a sustained layer, and check that the file's last samples are near zero for every toggle and choice setting.

flaws: The tail is a scatter of isolated ticks spread over the last ~0.7 s with gaps between them. It reads less like garment settle or drips and more like stray leftover events.
The zipper is buried. It shows as regular impulse striations inside the rustle bursts rather than as a distinct, readable zip gesture, so 'zipper presence' mostly thickens the rustle.
The water squeak is barely visible. Only faint steady horizontal dashes appear, and where they do show (tail=false) they look like a fixed synthetic tone rather than a pitch-sliding rubbery squeak.
Speed hardly changes overall duration. Min and max renders are both about 1.65–1.69 s, with the extra time filled by sparse tail, so the active gesture compresses but the file length does not.
Default silence of 25% is high for a continuous movement sound and comes mainly from the sparse tail.
grades.lesson: A one-shot's tail should be a continuous, intentional decay or a clearly motivated event. It should not be a sparse sprinkle of leftover particles, and file length should track the active gesture so a speed or density knob does not leave long, mostly empty endings.

brief: Loopable 2 s quiet back-alley drips and gutter trickle; knobs: container (bucket|dumpster|pipe), drip density 0..1, echo amount 0..1, distant city 0..1, drip rate, loop crossfade toggle
Body drop into street water; knobs: surface (puddle|wet asphalt|gutter), weight 0..1, splash 0..1, cloth slap 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The low-frequency body thud is not clearly separated from the broadband splash. The bottom band is hot but short and smeared into the noise, so 'weight' may read more as louder splash than heavier body.
The all-minimum render shows a second distinct burst around 0.7 s, which can read as a second impact or a bounce rather than settling water.
The droplet tail in the defaults and wet asphalt is sparse and somewhat evenly spaced, so it reads slightly synthetic. Wet asphalt is 43% silence.
With tail off, the onset ramps over about 50 ms before the peak, which is a little soft for a body hitting the ground.
grades.lesson: For compound impacts (body plus debris or splash), build the core impact as its own layer with a clear low-end transient that the weight knob scales in level, depth and length. Then make sure no range setting produces a secondary burst big enough to read as a second hit.

brief: Crosswalk push-button press with confirm tone; knobs: button (metal|plastic), click weight 0..1, confirm tone 0..1, wetness 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Metal and plastic barely differ. Plastic is only slightly shorter and duller (centroid 1586 vs 1277 Hz) with the same envelope and tone, so the material choice reads as a small EQ change, not a different button.
The all-maximum render looks almost the same as the defaults: similar length, RMS and tone lines. The upper ends of the ranges add little character.
The confirm tone is a plain steady sine-like line partly masked by the click cluster. It lacks the distinctive beep or chirp pattern of real crosswalk confirms.
With tail on, the tone decays slowly into a long, quiet ring-out. Much of the 0.95 s is low-level tail that a game team will probably trim.
grades.lesson: When a knob switches between materials or types, change the resonant structure and envelope (modal frequencies, decay time, transient sharpness), not just brightness or level, so each choice reads as a different object at a glance.

brief: Far thunder roll muffled by rain and buildings; knobs: size (small|medium|large), rumble depth 0..1, crack amount 0..1, roll length 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

warnings: slow: 2170 ms worst render

flaws: Every render starts at near-full amplitude on the first sample. Distant thunder muffled by buildings should swell in softly, with the roll building over a few hundred ms. As it stands it reads closer to a nearby burst that has been low-passed.
The roll is a single dense burst that decays in about 1.5 s. Real far thunder has several uneven swells and rumbles over 4-8 s. The 3 s default and 3.1 s 'all max' are short for a 'roll'.

The knob extremes barely change the shape. Small is 1.9 s, large is 3.5 s and roll length at max only reaches about 3.1 s, yet every render shows the same front-loaded decay. Large does not read as a bigger, longer, more rolling event.
tail=false still shows a long decaying tail (2.39 s versus 3.02 s). The toggle does not visibly do what its name says.
Crack amount at max only lifts the centroid to about 540 Hz with diffuse mid energy. There is no distinct crack transient that a designer could dial in or out.
grades.lesson: Make each knob's extremes produce an obviously different envelope or spectrum that matches its name. A 'length' or 'size' control should span a perceptually large range, and a toggle should remove or add what it says. Shape the attack to the source's distance: far-away events swell in, they do not start at full level.

flaws: Roll length does not work: every range at maximum (3.63 s) is shorter than every range at minimum (3.79 s), and nothing exceeds 3.90 s. The roll length knob is either inert or swamped by a hard duration cap.
Size large renders at the same 3.90 s as the default with a near-identical envelope, so large is barely distinct from medium. Only small changes noticeably.
tail=false appears truncated rather than designed: low-frequency energy still runs to the right edge of the spectrogram at 2.59 s, which reads as an abrupt end, not a short natural decay.

In every render the decay breaks into sparse, gated low-frequency fragments, visible as broken stutters at the end of the spectrogram. The tail sputters out instead of fading as a smooth, muffled rumble.
The defaults show a sharp broadband vertical line at onset. For thunder that is far and muffled by rain and buildings, the default crack should be softer or more low-passed.
Every seed and every setting has the same macro shape: one burst followed by a decay. Real distant rolls vary in the number and timing of their swells, so takes and sizes feel templated.
grades.lesson: When a knob controls duration (length, roll, tail), make sure the output buffer grows with it and the envelope reaches true silence. Render its min and max and check that the length actually moves in the stated direction and ends in a smooth fade, not a cap or a truncation.

flaws: tail=false appears to cut the sound off rather than shorten it: the waveform is still at clear amplitude at the 2.59 s end and the spectrogram shows energy right to the edge. That will click or chop in a scene.

The size choice barely differentiates. Large is the same 3.90 s as medium (the default), and its centroid (377 Hz) is higher than medium's (276 Hz) and almost equal to small's (375 Hz). Bigger thunder should get deeper and longer, not brighter.

At every-range-max the centroid jumps to 731 Hz and the spectrogram shows hard vertical crack stripes up the spectrum. That reads as a close strike, not 'far, muffled by rain and buildings'. The crack range overshoots the brief.
The default render shows a faint broadband vertical line at the onset. For heavily muffled distant thunder, the first crack should be low-passed as much as the roll.
grades.lesson: When a knob is a switch or a size class, each setting must move the sound in the physically expected direction: a larger source gets lower and longer, never brighter or the same length. Any toggle that shortens a sound must apply a proper fade-out, never truncate the buffer while signal is still present.

brief: Hand or object slamming a wet car hood; knobs: panel (hood|roof|trunk), force 0..1, metal ring 0..1, water spray 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the metal ring is hard to see. The spectrogram shows broadband noise and a low band but almost no tonal partials, so the hood reads more as a generic thump-and-hiss than sheet metal until ring is pushed up.
The low-frequency band lingers to about 0.9 s at defaults, longer than a real hood slam, which is a short boom and a quick decay. This leans slightly toward a wash.
Water spray is only a high-frequency noise burst fused to the onset. There are no scattered droplet transients after the impact, so 'wet' is weakly conveyed.
hood and roof are nearly identical in envelope and spectrum (centroid 943 vs 1018 Hz). Only trunk reads as clearly different.
The minimum extreme is quite dull and quiet (centroid 372 Hz). It is usable as a soft tap, but it loses most of the metal character.
grades.lesson: When a sound is a composite of named layers (thud, metal ring, water spray), make each layer visibly identifiable at default settings, e.g. tonal partials for metal and scattered transients for droplets, rather than relying on knob extremes to reveal them. Defaults are what buyers audition first.

brief: Pedestrian crossing chirp/tick signal; knobs: tone (chirp|tick|beep), pitch, rate, brightness 0..1, rain wash 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Default render has an audible broadband 'rain wash' noise bed filling the gaps between chirps. A signal device should default dry, with the ambience opt-in, since designers will layer their own street bed.
In beep mode the tail smears into a continuous low tone that never drops out between beeps. The pulsed beeps read as beeps riding on a drone rather than discrete pulses.
Default tail places a strong delayed ghost chirp halfway between each real chirp. Depending on rate, this can be mistaken for an extra signal pulse and muddy the rhythm.
Seeds differ only in noise and echo detail; the chirp shape, timing and pitch are identical. That is acceptable for a mechanical device but gives little take-to-take variety.
At maximum, the rate packs about 16 bright chirps into 1.5 seconds. This is near the edge of reading as a buzz rather than a crossing signal.
grades.lesson: Keep environmental layers (rain, room, traffic beds) and reverb or echo tails off or subtle at default for a source sound. Make sure any tail decays fully between repeats, so the core event stays clean and countable and the designer adds context deliberately.

brief: Downspout overflow pouring onto pavement; knobs: pipe material (tin|plastic|iron), pour volume 0..1, splash spread 0..1, metallic ring 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a ~2.2 s broadband noise burst with a fade, not a downspout overflow. The spectrogram is evenly smeared hiss with no gurgle or bubble structure, no chunky low-mid splash on pavement, and no stream-versus-impact layering. It reads as generic filtered noise.

The metallic ring shows up as thin, isolated steady sine lines that appear mostly after the water stops. That reads as synthetic tones pasted onto the tail rather than a pipe resonating under flow, and on iron it becomes a stray low drone line.

tail=false cuts off at full amplitude at 2.1 s. The waveform drops from peak to nothing instantly, which will click. It is also not a usable loop, because the start is abrupt too and nothing shows the ends were matched.

The default starts at full level with no onset shaping, so it neither eases in as a pour nor attacks as an event. A continuous overflow should be a sustained, loopable bed or a clearly shaped one-shot, and this is neither.

Material changes are subtle. Tin, plastic and iron share near-identical bodies, and the difference lives almost entirely in faint tail tones, so the headline choice knob barely changes the main sound.
Seeds are distinct but differ only in fine noise detail. That is acceptable, but it confirms the body is unstructured noise.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes part of an envelope, such as a tail, release or fade, the remaining sound must still end cleanly: apply a short fade-out or design it as a sample-matched loop. Never let a knob turn a shaped sound into one that ends at full amplitude.

flaws: Overflow from a downspout is a sustained event, but the pour body is a fixed ~2.2 s one-shot that swells in and fades out. There is no duration or loop control, so it cannot cover a continuous storm scene.

The three pipe materials barely differ. Centroids are 1297/1105/1063 Hz, and the spectrograms show nearly the same broadband wash. Only iron shows faint horizontal ring partials, so the headline choice knob does little to the stream's character.
Metallic ring at maximum adds only faint tonal lines buried under the noise. 'Pipe ring' never reads as a distinct, resonant pipe tone.
With tail=false the sound holds full level and then fades over a very short span. It reads as cut off rather than a pour stopping.
The minimum render becomes sparse isolated clicks rather than a thin trickle. Low pour volume reads as random drips instead of a weak continuous stream.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a continuous or ongoing phenomenon, build a sustained, loop-friendly body with a duration control, not a fixed one-shot swell. A selectable material or type should change the spectrum enough to be obvious in the picture (distinct resonances or brightness), not just nudge the centroid by 10-15%.

flaws: The default plays as a swell-and-fade one-shot of about 2 s of pour, then sparse drips. A real overflow is a steady pour, so the steady version is only available through tail=false.

The material choices barely separate spectrally. Plastic and iron both measure about 1075 Hz centroid. Iron mainly differs by an odd two-surge envelope rather than a heavier, lower ring. Tin vs plastic shows only faint differences in the horizontal ring lines.
With tail=false the render stays at full level and stops dead at 3 s. That is usable as loop material, but it is a hard cut if dropped in as a one-shot. There is no loop-safe crossfade.
The minimum-range render thins into granular spatter with a 26% silence fraction. It reads closer to a light drip than an overflow.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names physical materials, make each option move the spectrum measurably (resonant frequency, decay, brightness). Do not rely on changing the level or the envelope shape. If two options produce near-identical centroids, the choice is cosmetic.

brief: Interface blip styled as a neon buzz pop for menus; knobs: variant (select|back|error), buzz 0..1, brightness 0..1, drip accent 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults run 0.63 s with a long low decaying tail. That is too long and too dull for a menu blip: the centroid is about 1.5 kHz, energy is concentrated low in the spectrogram, and a menu sound wants a bright pop well under 0.3 s.
The all-minimum render collapses to a 466 Hz low thump with almost no upper spectrum. It reads as a soft kick or knock, not a neon buzz.
'back' is barely distinguishable from 'select': it has the same envelope and the same drip chirps, just slightly darker. A designer could not tell confirm from cancel by ear.

'tail = false' does more than shorten the sound. It changes the whole character: denser sustained buzz bursts, a much hotter RMS (0.171 against about 0.11), and the drip chirps become prominent rising tones. The toggle behaves like a different preset, not a tail switch.
The 'drip' accents show as late rising chirps around 0.25–0.3 s. They stack onto the tail and smear the pop instead of punctuating it.
The 'error' variant is the clearest of the three variants (it plays as triple pulses), but it is still long at 0.74 s for UI feedback.
grades.lesson: For UI sounds, make the default render short and bright, so the brief's sound is what plays at defaults. Each toggle should change only the property it is named for, so that turning off a tail shortens the sound without rebalancing or re-voicing everything else.

flaws: The drip accent is hard to see at defaults. The select variant shows no clear falling or rising pitch gesture, so the 'drip' in the title barely reads unless the variant is back.
The buzz character is fairly tame. The default spectrogram shows a few sparse harmonic lines rather than the dense, gritty harmonic stack a 'neon buzz' implies.
The default select render opens with a soft, rounded pre-blip before the main pop. This blunts the snappy onset expected of a menu confirm, and the first 70 ms read as a swell rather than a click.
All ranges at minimum collapse to a fairly dull low-mid tone (centroid 1427 Hz), which drifts toward a muffled thud rather than a bright UI blip.
grades.lesson: When a knob or a word in the title promises a specific gesture (a drip, a sweep, a zap), make that gesture clearly visible in the default render. Do not leave it to appear only in one variant or at the knob's extreme, because buyers judge the sound by its defaults.

brief: Two mugs clinking in a toast; knobs: material (pewter|ceramic|wood), force 0..1, liquid slosh 0..1, pitch, room tail toggle

flaws: The room tail toggle barely reads. The render grows from 0.59 s to 0.92 s, but the waveform and spectrogram show almost no added diffuse tail. The extra length is mostly silence (57%), so the toggle feels like padding rather than a space.
Liquid slosh is hard to find even at the maximum extreme. There is only a bit of mid-band noise smear and one late blip, with no clear low, wet, irregular texture after the clink.
There is no visible double impact or flam of two mugs meeting. Each render is a single strike, which undersells 'two mugs clinking'.
The all-minimum render collapses to one clean tonal line with a soft onset. It reads more like a struck bell or chime than a mug clink.
At defaults, about a third of the file is trailing near-silence, which adds dead time when editing.
grades.lesson: When a toggle or knob adds a layer (reverb tail, slosh, debris), make that layer clearly visible in the render as its own energy region, not just extra file length or a few dB of smear. If you can't point to it in the spectrogram, the buyer won't hear it in a mix.

brief: Heavy mug slammed down on an oak table; knobs: mug material (pewter|ceramic|wood), force 0..1, table resonance 0..1, liquid splash 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: tail=false trims the file from 0.89 s to 0.59 s, but the ring-out does not get shorter. Its decay looks as long as or longer than the default, so the toggle mostly crops trailing silence instead of damping the resonance.

All-minimum render loses the slam. Peak drops to 0.43 and the low-end thud thins out, leaving a light tap with two sustained tonal partials ringing for about 0.5 s. That reads closer to a struck bell than a mug set down on oak.
Liquid splash at maximum shows no distinct noisy, wet burst after the impact. It blends into a broadband smear, so the knob's character is hard to identify.
Defaults carry 58% trailing silence (about 0.5 s of padding after a roughly 0.35 s event), which wastes file length for a one-shot.

Material choices are distinguishable (pewter has a mid ring, ceramic a higher partial, wood is duller and lower in centroid). Seeds vary partial frequencies sensibly while keeping the same envelope. The core impact is a credible first pass.
grades.lesson: A toggle that claims to remove a tail must shorten the actual decay (damp the resonators or apply a faster release), not just truncate the render length. Verify that its 'off' state has a visibly shorter energy envelope than 'on', not merely less trailing silence.

brief: Wet metal trash can knocked over on pavement; knobs: can material (steel|plastic|dumpster lid), force 0..1, rattle 0..1, water slosh 0..1, pitch, reverb tail toggle

flaws: The 'wet' half of the brief is invisible at defaults. There is no broadband slosh or splash layer anywhere in the spectrogram, so it reads as a dry metal clatter, not a wet can on pavement.
Defaults show a hit, a couple of bounces and a tonal ring-out, but no clear roll/wobble settle. That settle is the signature of a toppled can, as opposed to a struck one.
The roll/wobble pulsing only shows up in the tail=false render. A reverb toggle should not change the impact choreography.
The all-minimum render has a soft, swelling attack that peaks about 0.1 s in, plus a steady low drone band. It reads as a muffled thump with hum, not a light knock-over.
The steel default centroid of about 730 Hz is dull for a thin steel can. The high-frequency clank and scrape on pavement is weak, so steel and dumpster lid differ mostly in loudness and low end.
The seeds vary only slightly. Bounce timing and count are nearly identical across seeds 1–3, so repeated triggers in a scene would sound copy-pasted.
grades.lesson: Every noun and adjective in the brief (here 'wet' and 'knocked over') must produce its own visible layer or event in the default render. A defining element should never exist only as an optional knob or be hidden behind an unrelated toggle.

flaws: At minimum settings the onset is not a hard hit. The waveform swells to its peak over roughly 0.1 s and becomes a rounded low blob. A gentle topple should still start with a sharp strike, just quieter and duller.
The water slosh is hard to identify in any render. There is no distinct wet, noisy, low-mid splash layer, so the 'wet' part of the brief is barely visible.
The defaults show little pavement scrape after the initial impacts. Most of the 1.7 s is tonal ringing and decay, not the can tumbling and settling.
The plastic setting still carries fairly defined ringing partials in its tail. It reads closer to thin metal than hollow plastic.
With the reverb tail off, the end of the sound is choppy. It reads as a rolling can, but the periodic bursts are quite regular and synthetic-looking.
grades.lesson: Keep the attack of an impact sound instantaneous at every knob extreme. Low force or intensity should lower level, brightness and bounce count, never stretch the onset into a swell, because a soft-attack impact reads as a different, wrong sound.

brief: Mallet driving a spigot into a barrel bung; knobs: barrel size (keg|hogshead|tun), strike force 0..1, liquid fullness 0..1, hit count, tail toggle

flaws: The strikes in a sequence are near-identical in pitch and damping. Driving a spigot in should audibly progress: the bung seats, the knock tightens and gets duller and shorter. Here the third hit looks like a copy of the first.
At the all-minimum setting the single hit rings almost as a pure low sine with little woody attack noise. It reads closer to a tom or bottle thump than oak being struck.
The tail toggle adds a fairly generic broadband wash rather than the barrel's own body ring. It is usable but undistinguished.
grades.lesson: When a sound repeats an action that changes the object (driving, tightening, filling, breaking), make each hit evolve across the sequence (pitch, damping, brightness) instead of retriggering one strike with random jitter. Otherwise the take reads as a loop rather than a process.

brief: Café door opens, bell jingles, rain swells in then muffles; knobs: bell (brass|tin|chime), door force 0..1, rain swell 0..1, interior warmth 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: slow: 1058 ms worst render

flaws: Rain does not swell in. The broadband noise starts at full level on the first strike and decays with the bell, so it reads as a cymbal-like wash glued to the hit rather than rain growing as the door opens.

Rain does not muffle. After the second event the noise simply disappears instead of continuing as a dense, low-passed bed behind the closed door. The scene empties to a bare bell tail with about 13% silence.
The bell is not a jingle. Each event is a single strike with sustained horizontal partials, not a cluster of rapid small-bell transients, so it reads as a struck bell or chime, not a café door bell.

No door-open event is visible at the start: there is no latch click, creak or low-frequency push before the bell. The only door-like thump is the low burst at the second event, which reads as the close.
With rain swell at its minimum the rain layer nearly vanishes, which suggests rain is a decoration on the strikes rather than an independent ambience layer.
Brass, tin and chime are clearly distinct, and the seeds look like two takes of the same sound. The weakness is the scene construction, not the bell synthesis.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes how a layer evolves over time (swells in, then muffles), give that layer its own independent envelope and filter path, separate from the transient events. Then check the spectrogram to confirm the layer rises, persists and changes timbre as described, rather than just decaying along with the hits.

flaws: The rain does not swell in. Its broadband noise starts abruptly with the door transient and decays on the same curve as the bell, so it reads as a noise burst attached to the hit, not weather pouring in through an open door.

Rain is nearly gone before the second (closing) event at every setting. The 'swell then muffle' arc the brief asks for, loud while open and then low-passed after the close, never happens; there is nothing left to muffle.

The bell strikes once per event, with a few stable partials. A café door bell jingles as several quick irregular strikes; only 'tin' hints at clatter, and 'brass' and 'chime' sound like single struck tones.
There is a gap of about 0.2 s before the first event, which wastes the head of the file for anyone syncing to picture.
At maximum, the closing event is so quiet that it barely registers as a second door action.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes a layer with its own time arc (swells in, persists, then muffles), give that layer an independent envelope and filter automation spanning the whole event. Do not drive it from the same decay as the transient, or it collapses into part of the hit.

flaws: The bell, the title element, reads as a few steady horizontal partials. There is no jingle: no clustered, irregular clapper strikes and no beating between detuned bells. It will sound like held synth tones, not a shop bell swinging on a door.
Bell partials are buried under the broadband rain swell during the open phase. The bell should sit on top of the mix, but the rain dominates the spectrogram's hot region.

The bell appears only twice, once at open and once at close, each as a single static chord. A real door bell keeps ringing and rattling as the door swings, so the second hit should be a decaying flurry, not another clean sustained chord.

The bell = brass/tin/chime choices differ mainly in partial spacing and centroid (1932 to 2311 Hz). The envelope and strike pattern are identical across all three, so the choices feel like EQ presets rather than different hardware.
Seeds vary noise texture and transient height but the bell partials sit at nearly the same frequencies in every take. Two takes of a jingling bell should differ in strike timing and count.
grades.lesson: When a brief names an articulated event (jingle, rattle, clatter, crackle), build it from multiple irregularly timed, individually decaying strikes rather than one sustained tone. The hero element of the title must also stay audibly on top of any bed layer like rain or room tone.

brief: Ale poured from a barrel tap into a mug; knobs: vessel size (small|tankard|pitcher), flow rate 0..1, foam fizz 0..1, fill duration, tail toggle

flaws: The pour body is a near-uniform broadband noise wash centred around 2.3 kHz. It shows little of the bubbly, gurgling granular structure of real liquid, so it risks reading as hiss rather than ale.
The rising cavity-resonance line, the key 'vessel filling' cue, is present but faint and buried in the noise.
tail=false ends with the body at full amplitude and then a hard cut at 1.78 s. That is an abrupt stop, not a tap closing.

The vessel choices (small, tankard, pitcher) look and measure very alike: only a modest centroid shift, the same length, and the same pitch-sweep shape. Vessel size should change the resonance range and the fill time noticeably.
The tail drips and fizz after the pour are sparse and thin. The foam fizz could be more evident as a dense high crackle.
grades.lesson: Never end a sustained layer with a hard cut when an optional section is toggled off. Always apply a short release envelope so the sound closes naturally instead of truncating at full level.

brief: Barrel dropped upright onto planks; knobs: barrel size (keg|hogshead|tun), drop height 0..1, fullness slosh 0..1, hoop rattle 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Keg and hogshead (the default) are nearly indistinguishable: centroid is 1019 Hz vs 988 Hz and length 0.82 s vs 0.90 s. Only the tun reads as a clearly bigger, darker barrel (564 Hz, 1.02 s).
Hoop rattle shows up as steady horizontal tonal lines, i.e. clean ringing partials. A loose hoop should give a buzzy, irregular, decaying rattle.
Fullness slosh leaves no visible trace. There is no late, low, irregular liquid movement after the impact, so the knob's identity is unclear in the renders.

The impact is a single clean transient with no secondary bounce or settle. A heavy barrel landing upright on planks usually rocks or double-hits, so the result reads a little like a generic woody thump.
With every range at its minimum, the sound is very dull (366 Hz) and weak. It is still usable, but it loses the plank-crack attack.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names discrete sizes or types, make each option differ clearly in pitch, decay length and body resonance. Two options that render almost identically waste the knob and mislead buyers.

brief: Barrel rolled across floorboards; knobs: barrel size (keg|hogshead), fullness 0..1, floor creak 0..1, roll speed, tail toggle

flaws: Board-seam impacts look fairly irregular at defaults. A barrel rolling over evenly spaced floorboards should give a steadier thump rhythm tied to roll speed, so the roll reads a little more like random clatter than rotation.

The default centroid of 832 Hz is somewhat bright for a wooden barrel. The low-end body is present but the mid-high noise wash dilutes the weight, especially in the all-minimum render (1288 Hz), which sounds thin and hissy.
Floor creak is barely visible at defaults. Tonal creak lines only show clearly at the range maximum, so the default creak value may be too low to be useful.
Every seed ends with a similar late bump in the same position. This is acceptable, but the ending is less varied than the body.
grades.lesson: When a sound is driven by a physical mechanism such as rotation, steps or seams, derive the timing of its periodic impacts from the physical parameters (for example circumference and speed). That way the rhythm reads as the mechanism rather than as random transients scattered over noise.

brief: Bench dragged back from a table; knobs: bench length (stool|short|long), drag speed 0..1, floor grit 0..1, weight 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At default drag speed the scrape is mostly flat broadband noise reaching the top of the spectrum, with only faint low resonance bands. It has little of the stick-slip judder or tonal leg-chatter that sells wood dragging on a floor. That chatter only appears as vertical striations at the minimum range.
A near-silent gap sits between the end of the drag and the final knock, so the stop reads slightly as a separate lift-and-drop event rather than the bench coming to rest.
The drag segment has no clear acceleration or deceleration shape. Its envelope is a fairly even block of noise rather than a pull that starts, catches and slows.
Bench length mostly changes duration and thud pitch. The stool and long variants share nearly the same scrape texture, with no sense of more legs or more mass in the drag itself.
grades.lesson: Friction and scrape sounds should be built from stick-slip impulses or rate-modulated grains exciting a resonant body, with the modulation present at default settings; plain filtered noise with an envelope reads as hiss rather than an object rubbing on a surface.
